sections.title: Mate
sections.summary: The drink that runs the country

classes.title: What is mate?
classes.summary: A bitter leaf, a gourd and an invitation

pages.text: **Mate** is hot water poured over **yerba**, dried and ground leaves. You sip it from a small gourd through a metal straw, then it gets refilled and passed on.

pages.prompt: Yerba looks a lot like green tea. What plant is it really?
options: A green tea bush from China
A wild mint from the Andes
pages.explain: A holly. A totally different plant from tea, but it does have caffeine. That's why half the country runs on it.

pages.text: The gourd is also called a **mate**. And you don't drink mate here: you **tomás mate**.
The **Guaraní** drank yerba long before the Spanish arrived. Later, **Jesuit** missions tamed the wild plant and grew it on plantations.

pages.prompt: In 1767 the Jesuits were expelled. What happened to their yerba plantations?
options: Nobody could grow yerba for a century
Spain took them over and got rich
They moved the plants to Brazil
pages.explain: The trick to sprouting the seeds was lost. Yerba went back to being picked wild until growers cracked it again in the early 1900s. Most still comes from **Misiones** and **Corrientes**.

pages.text: By law, mate is Argentina's **infusión nacional**: the national drink. Not bad for a leaf you share with total strangers.
Someone holds up a gourd and asks **¿Tomás mate?** Say **dale**, sure. You just joined the round.

classes.title: The gear
classes.summary: Gourd, bombilla, termo and yerba: your starter kit

pages.text: The kit: a **mate** (the gourd), a **bombilla** (a metal straw with a filter at the bottom), a **termo** of hot water, and a pack of **yerba**.
The classic mate is a dried gourd, but there are wooden, glass and steel ones too. The chunky leather-wrapped one is the **mate camionero**: the trucker's mate.

pages.prompt: You just bought a beautiful new gourd. What do you do before your first mate?
options: Fill it with wet yerba and wait a day
Scrub it well with hot soapy water
Leave it out in the sun for a week
pages.explain: That's **curar el mate**, curing it. And never use soap: the gourd soaks it up, and so does your next mate.

pages.text: The bombilla goes in once and stays put. It's not a spoon, and never, ever a stirring stick.
Argentine termos come with a special spout, the **pico cebador**. It pours a thin, steady stream right next to the bombilla, without flooding the yerba.

pages.prompt: You open a pack of yerba and it's full of little sticks. Good or bad?
pages.explain: That's **yerba con palo**: milder, and slower to wash out. **Sin palo**, just leaves, hits harder. First time? Grab con palo.

pages.text: Pick your yerba brand carefully. People are fiercely loyal to theirs, and they'll happily tell you why yours is wrong.

classes.title: How to cebar
classes.summary: The montañita, the right water and the fool's first mate

pages.text: **Cebar** is to prepare and serve mate. The person doing it is the **cebador**. Small job, big status: a bad cebador hears about it all afternoon.
Fill the gourd about ¾ with yerba. Cover it, flip it, shake, then tilt it. The yerba settles into a slope: the **montañita**, the little mountain.

pages.prompt: How hot should the water be?
pages.explain: Boiling water **quema la yerba**: it burns it, and the mate turns harsh and bitter. Many electric kettles in Argentina even have a “mate” setting.

pages.text: Pour into the low side, next to the bombilla, and keep the top of the montañita dry. Some cebadores do it differently, and they'll defend it to the death.

pages.prompt: Who usually drinks the very first mate?
pages.explain: The first one is bitter, foamy and full of dust. The cebador takes the hit.

pages.text: There's a saying for it: **el primero es para el zonzo**, the first one's for the fool. A small sacrifice, not a privilege.
After many rounds the flavor fades and the mate is **lavado**: washed out. Time for fresh yerba.

classes.title: The rules of the ronda
classes.summary: Mate etiquette, so nobody gives you the look

pages.text: One mate, one bombilla, one **ronda**. The cebador fills it and hands it to you. You drink all of it, until it gurgles.

pages.prompt: You finish your mate. Who do you hand it to?
pages.explain: Always back to the cebador, who refills it for the next person. The mate never skips the cebador.

pages.text: Only the cebador touches the yerba and the bombilla. Fixing someone's mate is like rearranging their kitchen while they cook.

pages.prompt: You hand the mate back and say **“gracias”**. What happens next?
options: You get the next one first
pages.explain: In a ronda, **gracias** means “I'm done”. Want more? Just hand it back, maybe with a **¡qué rico!**

pages.text: Don't hold the mate while you tell a long story. Everyone's waiting and the water's getting cold. Someone will say **“¡No es un micrófono!”**
Don't wipe the bombilla before you drink. Sharing it is the whole point, and wiping it reads as “you think I'm dirty”.
Got a cold, or just don't feel like it? Say **“no, gracias”** the first time it comes your way. Nobody minds, and nobody asks why.

classes.title: Mate every day
classes.summary: Sweet or bitter, cold or in a cup, everywhere you go

pages.text: Most people drink it **amargo**: bitter, no sugar. **Mate dulce** has sugar, and it's more common in some families and provinces. Purists will tease you. Lovingly.
Old folklore says a mate could carry a message: sweet meant friendship, very hot meant passion, bitter meant indifference. Today it just means someone forgot the sugar.
**Mate cocido** is the cozy, lazy version: yerba in a tea bag, in a regular cup, often with milk. The drink of school breakfasts and the afternoon **merienda**.

pages.prompt: On a road trip, who makes the mate?
pages.explain: The co-pilot is the cebador. Keep them coming, and don't burn the driver.

pages.text: Mate goes everywhere: the office, university, the park, the beach. **Matear** is to drink mate together, and the **matera** is the bag that carries the kit.

pages.prompt: Up north, in 40 °C heat, what do people drink instead of hot mate?
options: Mate with ice-cold water or juice
Hot mate anyway, no matter what
pages.explain: That's **tereré**: cold water or juice, ice and herbs. Huge in Paraguay and in hot provinces like Corrientes, Misiones, Chaco and Formosa.

pages.text: In Buenos Aires, though, hot mate never takes a vacation. Even at the beach in January, someone has the termo.

classes.title: Mate next door
classes.summary: Uruguay, southern Brazil and a surprise buyer far away

pages.text: Argentina doesn't own mate. **Uruguay**, **Paraguay** and southern **Brazil** drink it every day too, and each one is sure its way is the right way.

pages.prompt: Which country drinks the most mate per person?
pages.explain: Uruguay, even more than Argentina. In Montevideo people carry the **termo bajo el brazo**, under the arm: to work, to the beach, along the rambla.

pages.text: The twist: Uruguay grows almost no yerba. Most of it comes from **Brazil**, ground fine, almost without stems. Stronger, more bitter, and full of dust.
Paraguay has its own trophy: in 2020 UNESCO listed its **tereré** culture, cold yerba with medicinal herbs, as world intangible heritage.
In southern Brazil, the gaúchos drink **chimarrão**: bright green, powder-fine yerba in a big gourd called a **cuia**. Same ronda, different accent.

pages.prompt: Which country buys the most yerba from Argentina?
pages.explain: Syria, year after year, by a long way. Uruguay buys mostly from Brazil.

pages.text: The link is people. Around 1900 many Syrians and Lebanese moved to Argentina, and some went home with the habit. Today the **Druze** of Syria and Lebanon especially love it.

sections.title: Asado
sections.summary: Fire, meat and a whole Sunday with your people

classes.title: More than a barbecue
classes.summary: Why an asado is a whole afternoon, not a meal

pages.text: An **asado** is grilled meat, sure. But mostly it's an excuse to spend the whole day together. **¿Hacemos un asado?** really means: want to hang out?

pages.prompt: The invite says **“Vení a la una.”** Come at one. When will you probably eat?
pages.explain: The fire is slow, and so is everything else. Have a drink by the grill and eat when the asador says so.

pages.text: Every asado has one **asador**, in charge of the fire and the meat. It's a role with a lot of pride. Everyone else keeps them company by the grill, drink in hand.
An asado is also how Argentines celebrate almost anything: a birthday, a win, a new job, a Friday.

pages.prompt: Builders just poured the concrete roof of a new house. What does the owner traditionally pay for?
options: An asado for the whole crew
A day off for the whole crew
A cash bonus for the foreman
pages.explain: The **asado de la losa**, for the finished roof slab. The crew grills right there on site, on bricks and a scrap of iron grate.

pages.text: For lots of families it's a weekly date: **el asado del domingo**. Same backyard, same asador, same arguments.
**Asado** is also the name of a cut: the ribs. So yes, you can eat asado at an asado.

classes.title: Playing with fire
classes.summary: Embers, firewood, salt and how you like it

pages.text: The **parrilla** is the grill: an iron grate, often built into the backyard in brick. Plenty of city apartments have a little one on the balcony. Priorities.
No balcony? Lots of apartment buildings have a **quincho**: a shared room with a parrilla, often on the roof. Neighbors book it for the weekend.

pages.prompt: What's the secret of a good asado fire?
options: No flames under the meat at all
Tall flames, for a crispy outside
A lid on top, to trap the smoke
pages.explain: You cook over **brasas**, embers. The asador burns wood off to one side and shovels embers under the grill, little by little. Flames burn the outside and leave the inside raw.

pages.text: **Leña**, firewood, takes longer, but many swear it tastes better. **Carbón**, charcoal, is faster, so most city asados use it. Ask two Argentines which is best: three opinions.

pages.prompt: What does the asador put on the meat before it hits the grill?
pages.explain: Usually just **sal gruesa**, coarse salt. Good meat and good embers do the rest. Chimichurri waits at the table.

pages.text: Then patience. The big cuts cook slowly, often for an hour and a half or more, and a good asador flips each one only once.
How do you like it? Most Argentines say **a punto**, medium, or **jugoso**, a bit pink. Ask for it very rare and you'll get a raised eyebrow.

classes.title: What comes off the grill, and when
classes.summary: Picada, sausages, achuras, then the big cuts

pages.text: While the fire does its thing, there's a **picada**: cheese, salami, olives, bread. It keeps everyone alive. Don't fill up, though. There's a long way to go.

pages.prompt: How much meat does the host buy per person?
pages.explain: Half a kilo each is the classic rule, bones included. Nobody wants to be the host who ran out.

pages.text: First off the grill: **chorizo** and **morcilla**. They get cut up on a board and passed around, often on a piece of bread.

pages.prompt: The morcilla is dark, soft and a little sweet. What's it made with?
pages.explain: Blood sausage. Sounds scary, tastes amazing. Saying **no, gracias** is fine too.

pages.text: Then the brave stuff, the **achuras**: **chinchulines**, crispy grilled intestines, and **mollejas**, sweetbreads, crispy outside and creamy inside. Try the mollejas with lemon.
Finally the main event: **asado de tira** (short ribs), **vacío** (flank) and **entraña** (skirt steak). The asador decides the order. Your job: eat, and say **¡qué rico!**
**Matambre a la pizza**: a thin flat cut, grilled until tender, then topped with tomato sauce and cheese right on the grill. Yes, pizza on the parrilla.

classes.title: Choripán, provoleta and the sauces
classes.summary: The sandwich, the grilled cheese and what goes on top

pages.text: **Choripán**: a grilled chorizo split open in a crusty roll. That's it, and it's perfect. Everyone calls it **chori**.
Ask for it **mariposa**, butterfly: the chorizo is split lengthwise and opened flat, so it cooks faster and crisps up.

pages.prompt: It's 5 a.m. and the boliche just closed. Where do porteños go for a chori?
options: A food stall by the river
pages.explain: The **carritos de la Costanera**, grill stalls along the river that barely ever close. Smoke, a line, and chimichurri dripping everywhere.

pages.text: Chori is street food everywhere: outside football stadiums, at every festival, and at political rallies.

pages.prompt: Critics sometimes call rally crowds **choripaneros**. What's the jab?
options: They only came for a free chori
The rally was held at a parrilla
pages.explain: The insult says people were brought in with a free sandwich, not real conviction. It's a political dig, so use it with care.

pages.text: **Provoleta** is a thick round of provolone-style cheese, grilled crispy outside and melty inside, with oregano and chili. Eat it fast, before it turns to rubber.
Two sauces rule. **Chimichurri** is green: parsley, oregano, garlic, chili flakes, vinegar and oil. **Salsa criolla** is tomato, onion and bell pepper.

classes.title: You're invited. Now what?
classes.summary: What to bring, how not to annoy the asador, and the applause

pages.text: The host buys the meat. Guests bring **vino**, drinks, dessert or **hielo**. Someone always forgets the ice.

pages.prompt: Before anything reaches the table, who gets the first bites?
options: The kids, so they stop asking
The host's parents, out of respect
pages.explain: Hang out by the grill and the asador will pass you bits of chorizo or crackling on bread, straight off the fire. Company earns you snacks.

pages.text: Golden rule: don't tell the asador how to cook. Not “it needs more heat”, not “in my country we…”. And never touch the tongs.
Want to help? Ask **“¿Te ayudo en algo?”** and do exactly what you're told. Or just bring the asador a glass of wine.

pages.prompt: The meat's done and everyone has eaten. What does someone always call out?
options: A round of applause for the asador
A short speech from the host
A group photo for the family chat
pages.explain: **¡Un aplauso para el asador!** Everyone claps, even if the meat was a bit dry.

pages.text: When the asador calls **“¡A la mesa!”**, go right away. Letting the meat go cold while you finish a story is the real insult.
The asador cooked, so the others clear the table and wash up. Offer to help with the dishes: that's how you get invited back.

classes.title: Asados from the rest of the country
classes.summary: Lamb on a cross, beef in its hide and dinner in a plough disc

pages.text: Down south the star isn't beef. It's **cordero patagónico**: a whole lamb opened flat, wired to an iron cross and stuck in the ground beside the fire for hours.
The big-party version is **asado con cuero**: beef cooked with its hide on. The hide works like a pot, holding in the juices and fat.

pages.prompt: A festival poster says the **vaquillona con cuero** is served at 1 p.m. When did the cooks light the fire?
pages.explain: Twelve hours or more over the embers means starting the night before and taking turns. Someone always brings a guitar and a termo.

pages.text: The town of **Viale**, in Entre Ríos, throws a national festival for asado con cuero every year.
In the west it's **chivito**: young goat, grilled slowly over the embers. Mendoza and Neuquén each swear theirs is the best.

pages.prompt: Out in the **campo** there's a giant pan for the fire called **el disco**. What was it originally?
options: A plough disc from the farm
The rim of a cart wheel
pages.explain: A worn-out **disco de arado**, plough disc, with legs and handles welded on. Instant giant wok.

pages.text: Chicken, onions, peppers, chorizo and a splash of wine, all stewing together: **pollo al disco**. One disco feeds a crowd, everyone standing around it with bread.

sections.title: La mesa argentina
sections.summary: Empanadas, pizza, milanesas, and dinner at ten

classes.title: Dinner at ten
classes.summary: Late dinners, the merienda, and a bill that never comes

pages.text: Argentines eat late. Lunch around one, dinner around **ten**. Book a restaurant for eight and you'll have the waiters all to yourself.
What gets everyone through? The **merienda**: around five, a mini-breakfast of mate or coffee with toast or **facturas**. Skip it and you'll be starving by eight.
Kids keep the same hours. Near midnight, restaurants are full of families, with little ones running between the tables or asleep across two chairs.

pages.prompt: You finished eating an hour ago. Why hasn't the waiter brought the bill?
options: Bringing it unasked would be like kicking you out
Bills only come once the kitchen has closed
He's waiting for you to order a coffee first
pages.explain: The table is yours until you ask: **“¿Me traés la cuenta?”** Or catch the **mozo**'s eye and pretend to write in the air.

pages.text: That's why the **sobremesa** exists: the long chat after the meal, over coffee. It often lasts longer than the meal itself, and nobody rushes you.

pages.prompt: Six friends, one bill. You only had a salad, Tomi had the steak. How does the table usually pay?
options: Each person pays for their own dish
pages.explain: Among friends, the bill gets split evenly. Asking to pay only for your salad would sound a bit stingy.

pages.text: Everyone throwing money into one pot is **hacer una vaquita**. Nobody counts who ate the extra slice. Next time, it'll be you.

classes.title: Empanadas
classes.summary: A secret code in the fold, and a war between provinces

pages.text: Party for twenty or a lazy Sunday night, the answer is the same: **empanadas**, ordered by the **docena**, the dozen. Half-moons of dough, baked or fried, a different filling in each.

pages.prompt: A dozen empanadas arrive: four fillings, nothing written on them. How do you tell them apart?
options: By the pattern folded into the edge
By a little dot of color on top
By a number stamped into the dough
pages.explain: The braided edge, the **repulgue**, is a code. Each filling gets its own fold.

pages.text: There's no national code, though. Every shop and every grandma has her own system. If it's not on the box, just ask: **“¿Cuál es cuál?”**
The northwest takes this very seriously. **Salta** and **Tucumán** each claim the best empanada in the country, and neither will ever back down.

pages.prompt: So what's the big difference between a salteña and a tucumana?
pages.explain: Salteñas get little cubes of **papa**. Put potato in a tucumana and someone from Tucumán will explain your mistake for twenty minutes.

pages.text: On good menus you'll see **cortada a cuchillo**: beef chopped by hand, not ground. It keeps the filling juicy.
A good empanada is full of hot juice. Bite a corner first and lean over the plate. In Tucumán, many add a squeeze of lemon before each bite.

classes.title: Pizza porteña
classes.summary: Thick, cheesy, eaten standing up, with fainá on top

pages.text: Buenos Aires pizza is its own thing: thick, fluffy dough under a scandalous amount of cheese. The default order is a **muzza**: tomato, cheese, a few green olives.
Then there's the **fugazzeta**: a mountain of onion over cheese. Order it **rellena** and the cheese comes stuffed inside the dough too. Heavy? Completely.

pages.prompt: Porteños often put something on top of their slice of pizza. What is it?
pages.explain: It's **fainá**, a chickpea flatbread brought by Genoese immigrants. Pizza with fainá on top is pizza **a caballo**: on horseback.

pages.text: Add a glass of cheap, sweet **moscato** and you've got the old porteño trio: **moscato, pizza y fainá**.
**Avenida Corrientes**, the theater street, is also the pizza street. The famous pizzerías there stay packed until long after the last show.

pages.prompt: The play just ended and the pizzería is packed. What do porteños do?
options: Eat a slice standing at the counter
Take a number and wait an hour
Buy a pizza to eat in the theater
pages.explain: Eating **de parado** at the counter, a **porción** in your hand, is a classic. Faster, cheaper, and honestly more fun.

classes.title: Nonna's kitchen
classes.summary: Milanesas, Sunday pasta and ñoquis on the 29th

pages.text: Huge waves of Italian immigrants arrived in Argentina, and their kitchen became the national one. Grandma and grandpa are even **nona** and **nono**.
The home-cooked star is the **milanesa**: thin beef, breaded and fried. It's what kids ask for on their birthday, and what's waiting in every lunchbox the day after.

pages.prompt: The **milanesa a la napolitana** comes with ham, cheese and tomato sauce. Where was it born?
pages.explain: At a restaurant called **Nápoli**, near the Luna Park stadium. The story goes a cook burnt a milanesa and hid the damage under ham, cheese and sauce.

pages.text: Sunday lunch at the grandparents' often means homemade pasta with **tuco**, a tomato sauce that simmers all morning. Nobody leaves before the second helping.
On the **29th** of every month, many families eat **ñoquis**. The ritual: a banknote under your plate while you eat, for money and luck.

pages.prompt: Why the 29th?
options: By then the salary was gone, and gnocchi are cheap
Pasta factories gave away leftovers that day
Italian immigrants got their papers that day
pages.explain: That's the practical explanation: potatoes and flour, the cheapest dinner before payday. There's also an Italian legend of a saint who left gold under a poor family's plate. Many keep the banknote in their wallet until next month.

pages.text: Which is why a **ñoqui** is also someone on the public payroll who only shows up around the 29th. To get paid.

classes.title: Stews and corn
classes.summary: Winter pots, patriotic locro and corn in its husk

pages.text: When winter hits, Argentines go for a **guiso**, a hearty home stew. One pot, cheap cuts, whatever's in the fridge, and bread to wipe the plate.
The king of them all is **locro**: white corn, beans, squash and several meats, cooked for hours until it's thick.

pages.prompt: When do whole neighborhoods cook giant pots of locro?
options: On national holidays like 25 de mayo
On the first frost of every winter
At the end of the corn harvest
pages.explain: On **25 de mayo** and **9 de julio**, locro is the patriotic dish.

pages.text: Clubs, parishes and neighbors cook it in pots big enough to bathe in and sell it by the portion. Bring your own **tupper**, and come early.
Locro is no immigrant dish. It comes from the Andes, from long before Argentina existed. On top goes **quiquirimichi**, a spicy red fat.
The **carbonada** is beef, squash, corn and sweet potato, often with dried peaches. The showstopper version is served inside a whole baked pumpkin.

pages.prompt: From the northwest comes **humita en chala**, a sweet corn paste. What is it wrapped in?
pages.explain: Fresh corn grated into a paste, wrapped in the **chala**, the husk, tied up and boiled. You unwrap it at the table like a present.

classes.title: Helado
classes.summary: Italian roots, flavors called gustos, and ice cream by the kilo

pages.text: Italian immigrants brought their **helado**, and Argentines will tell you it's the best outside Italy. There's a **heladería** on every other corner, and people eat it even in winter.
Flavors are called **gustos**, and even the smallest cup gets two. Choosing them is serious business.

pages.prompt: Winter, 11 p.m., dinner at a friend's place is over. What does the host order?
options: Coffee and cake from a café
pages.explain: Helado comes to your door in a foam box: **un cuarto**, **medio** or **un kilo**. Any night, any season.

pages.text: A kilo takes up to four gustos, and it's gone before anyone mentions dieting. **Un cuarto** is for one person with self-control.
A heladería lives or dies by its **dulce de leche**, and the best ones offer it in several versions. With chocolate flakes, it's **dulce de leche granizado**.

pages.prompt: **Sambayón**, a classic flavor, has a surprising ingredient. What is it?
pages.explain: It's the Italian *zabaione*: egg yolks, sugar and sweet wine. A grown-up flavor. Probably your abuelo's favorite.

pages.text: Order a dulce de leche, a sambayón, and one fruit flavor so you can say you ate something healthy.

sections.title: Alfajores y dulces
sections.summary: Dulce de leche, kioscos and the snack that runs on sugar

classes.title: Dulce de leche and friends
classes.summary: The spread on everything, and the sweets it hangs out with

pages.text: **Dulce de leche** is milk and sugar cooked slowly for hours until thick and brown. On toast, in cakes, straight from the jar with a spoon at midnight.
Just don't call it caramel. Say that to an Argentine and watch their face fall.

pages.prompt: Legend says dulce de leche was invented by accident in 1829. How?
options: A maid forgot the milk on the stove
A soldier left sugar in his canteen
A baker burned a batch of flan
pages.explain: The story goes: a ranch in Cañuelas, the governor Rosas meeting his rival Lavalle to sign a truce, and a maid so caught up in the drama she forgot the pot.

pages.text: Cute story, almost certainly a legend. Uruguay, Chile, France and others claim dulce de leche too. Uruguay, loudly.
At the supermarket, **clásico** is soft, for toast and the spoon. **Repostero** is firmer, for baking: it holds its shape inside alfajores without dripping.

pages.prompt: The **chocotorta** is the classic birthday cake. How long does it spend in the oven?
pages.explain: Zero. Chocolinas cookies dipped in milk, layered with dulce de leche mixed with cream cheese. Into the fridge, done.

pages.text: Two more to know: **pastafrola**, a lattice tart with quince or sweet potato jam, and **Mantecol**, a peanut nougat bar people get weirdly emotional about.

classes.title: What is an alfajor?
classes.summary: Two cookies, dulce de leche in the middle, and a very long trip

pages.text: An **alfajor** is two soft cookies stuck together with a filling, usually dulce de leche, often dipped in chocolate. That's it. That's the whole religion.

pages.prompt: Where was the alfajor born?
pages.explain: The name comes from Andalusian Arabic. In al-Ándalus it was a honey, almond and spice sweet, and Andalucía still makes it today.

pages.text: The Spanish brought the name across the ocean, and here it became cookies plus dulce de leche. Argentina just, humbly, perfected it.
Every region has its own. **De maicena** is the one your abuela makes: crumbly cornstarch cookies, dulce de leche, edges rolled in grated coconut.
**Marplatense**: dipped in chocolate, the kiosco classic. **Santafesino**: crunchy layers, white sugar glaze. **Cordobés**: soft, glazed, often filled with fruit jam.

pages.prompt: Industry estimates count how many alfajores Argentines eat. How many a day?
pages.explain: About six million a day, by the industry's own estimate. That's roughly one for every eight people, every single day.

pages.text: Skipped lunch? Ask for a **triple**: three cookies, two layers of dulce de leche. More alfajor per alfajor.

classes.title: Brands, kioscos and the eternal debate
classes.summary: Havanna or Jorgito? Pick a side at the kiosco on the corner

pages.text: Every block has a **kiosco**: a tiny shop selling candy, drinks, phone credit and, above all, alfajores. Many stay open late, some never close: look for **24 hs**.

pages.prompt: The kiosco has no coins for your change. What might you get instead?
pages.explain: During years of coin shortages, **caramelos** became the unofficial small change. Some kioscos still do it.

pages.text: Some kioscos are literally a **ventanita**, a little window in someone's house. Knock, ask, pay, done.

pages.prompt: You're meeting your partner's family for the first time. Which alfajores do you bring?
pages.explain: **Havanna**, from Mar del Plata, is the fancy one: the box you bring as a gift.

pages.text: **Jorgito** and **Guaymallén** are the everyday kiosco heroes: cheap, humble, legendary. Beloved, but a coins-in-your-pocket snack, not a meet-the-parents gift.
Ask a table “which is the best alfajor?” and clear your afternoon. Some swear by Havanna. Others call it overpriced and grab a humble **Guaymallén**.
There's even a **Mundial del Alfajor**, held in Buenos Aires. A “world” championship for our own snack: peak Argentina.

classes.title: Facturas: anarchy at the bakery
classes.summary: Medialunas, bolas de fraile and the rebel bakers who named them

pages.text: **Facturas** are the sweet pastries from the **panadería**, bought by the dozen in a paper bag. Everyone mixes their own dozen, and everyone has a favorite.

pages.prompt: The queen is the **medialuna**, a small croissant. There are two kinds. How do you tell them apart at a glance?
options: Butter ones curve, fat ones are straight
Butter ones are twice as big
Fat ones have sesame on top
pages.explain: The old rule: **manteca curva, grasa recta**. Lots of bakeries still shape them that way.

pages.text: **De manteca**, with butter, is sweet and glazed. **De grasa**, with beef fat, is drier and a little salty. Which is better is a national debate.

pages.prompt: Pastries here have names like “friar's balls” and “nun's sighs”. Who named them, the story goes?
pages.explain: In 1887 Buenos Aires bakers, many of them Italian and Spanish anarchists, founded their first union. The story goes they named pastries to mock the Church, the army and the police.

pages.text: The **vigilante**, the cop, is long like a police baton. **Bolas de fraile** and **suspiros de monja** tease the Church. **Cañoncitos**, little cannons, go after the army.
Historians debate how much of this story is documented. But it's the one every baker will tell you.
Going to a friend's for mate in the afternoon? Stop at the panadería for **una docena de facturas**. Nobody has ever said no.

classes.title: ¿Qué hay de postre?
classes.summary: Flan mixto, a cop's dessert and the rest of the abuela's menu

pages.text: Sunday lunch is over and someone asks the big one: **¿qué hay de postre?** At home or at a **bodegón**, an old-school restaurant, the answer is a homemade classic.
**Flan** is egg custard with caramel. Here it rarely comes alone: with dulce de leche, with whipped cream, or both. Both is **mixto**, and it's the right answer.

pages.prompt: The bodegón menu offers **postre vigilante**. What arrives?
options: The long pastry from the bakery
Ice cream with dulce de leche
pages.explain: Also called **queso y dulce**: a slice of cheese with quince or sweet potato paste. The story goes police ordered it because it cost almost nothing.

pages.text: **Budín de pan** is bread pudding made from yesterday's bread, milk, eggs and caramel. Immigrant thrift turned into dessert.
**Arroz con leche** is rice slowly cooked in milk with sugar, lemon peel and cinnamon. It's also the name of a song every kid knows.

pages.prompt: What's the kids' song **“Arroz con leche”** actually about?
options: A kid sent to buy milk
pages.explain: **“Arroz con leche, me quiero casar…”**: rice pudding, I want to get married. It's a circle game. The pudding just opens the song.

pages.text: **Panqueques** here are thin crêpes rolled around dulce de leche. Some parrillas serve them **quemados**, with the sugar burnt crunchy on top.
Too full for the abuela's flan? Say **“un poquito nomás”**, just a little bit. Saying no is not an option.

sections.title: Fútbol
sections.summary: Not a sport here. A religion with a fixture list.

classes.title: ¿De qué cuadro sos?
classes.summary: The question you can't dodge, and the rivalries behind it

pages.text: Meet someone in Argentina and within ten minutes you'll hear it: **¿De qué cuadro sos?** Which team are you? Here a club is a **cuadro**.
Five clubs are **los cinco grandes**: Boca, River, Independiente, Racing and San Lorenzo. Everyone else is a “small” club. Just don't say that to their fans.
The biggest match of all is **Boca vs River**: the **Superclásico**. Two clubs that hate each other more than anything.

pages.prompt: So where was River born?
options: In La Boca, right next to Boca
In Núñez, where it plays today
pages.explain: Both clubs started in La Boca. River moved north later. Neighbors first, enemies forever.

pages.text: In 2018 they met in the Copa Libertadores final. Boca's bus was attacked on the way to the second leg, so the final was moved to **Madrid**. River won.

pages.prompt: Racing and Independiente are fierce rivals. How far apart are their stadiums?
pages.explain: You can see one stadium from the other. That's the **clásico de Avellaneda**: sharing a street with the team you hate most.

pages.text: Golden rule: never wear one club's colors near the other's stadium. Especially on match day.
No team? Don't fake one. Say **“No sé, ¿vos de cuál sos?”** and enjoy the next half hour of stories.

classes.title: La hinchada
classes.summary: Jumping stadiums, rock-song chants, cábalas and mufas

pages.text: A fan is a **hincha**. The whole crowd is **la hinchada**. They don't watch the match. They play it from the stands.
You don't pick a club. **You're born into it.** Lots of babies are signed up as club members before they can walk.

pages.prompt: Boca fans say their stadium, La Bombonera, “doesn't shake, it beats”, like a heart. Why?
options: The whole crowd jumps at the same time
It was built over an old stream
The club plays drums through the speakers
pages.explain: When the whole stadium jumps together, the stands really move. **“La Bombonera no tiembla, late.”**

pages.text: The singing never stops, and lots of the songs are old rock hits with new words. **“Brasil, decime qué se siente”** is sung to *Bad Moon Rising*.
Every rival gets a nickname. River fans call Boca fans **bosteros** (bosta = dung). Boca fans call River fans **gallinas**: chickens.

pages.prompt: Why are River fans called “gallinas”?
options: River blew a 2–0 lead in a big final
Their first stadium was a chicken farm
Their old jersey had feathers on it
pages.explain: In the 1966 Copa Libertadores final, River were winning 2–0 and lost 4–2. At the next match, rival fans threw a chicken onto the pitch. The name stuck.

pages.text: Hinchas are superstitious. Same seat, same socks, the shirt you never wash: that's a **cábala**. And if your team loses every time you show up, you're **mufa**: bad luck.

pages.prompt: Your friend's team lost the last 3 matches you watched together. Tonight is the big one. What happens?
options: He saves you the best spot on the couch
He asks you to watch it at your place
He lends you his lucky shirt
pages.explain: Nothing personal: you're **mufa**. Maybe you can come back next season.

pages.text: When River got relegated in 2011, their stadium stayed full in the second division. Loyalty like that has a name: **aguante**.

classes.title: Talk like a hincha
classes.summary: The potrero, the weekly picado, the previa and Monday's gastada

pages.text: Argentines say their football was born in the **potrero**: a dirt lot, two stones for goals, no rules. Calling a player **“de potrero”** is a big compliment.
Today the potrero is **fútbol 5**. Plenty of adults play a **picado** every week, with the same friends for years. Then beers.

pages.prompt: In a picado, you play the ball past your friend Nacho and everyone screams **“¡Caño!”**. What did you just do?
options: Put the ball between his legs
Kicked him instead of the ball
pages.explain: A **caño** is a nutmeg. No goal needed: Nacho will hear about it for weeks.

pages.text: The coach is **el DT**, the director técnico. And every Argentine is secretly a DT: they all know who should have played.
Before a big match you **hacer la previa**: meet early to eat, drink and sing. The previa often lasts longer than the match.

pages.prompt: It's Monday. Your team lost 4–0 yesterday. What's waiting for you at the office?
options: Nobody mentions it, out of respect
Memes, jokes, and a rival's shirt on your chair
pages.explain: Welcome to the **gastada**.

pages.text: The **gastada** is the teasing after a loss. You take it, you save the memes, and you pay it back when you win. “It's only a game” is not an accepted answer.

classes.title: The table, the drop and the VAR
classes.summary: Irse a la B, the promedios and endless penalty debates

pages.text: Every club's nightmare is the **descenso**: relegation. Argentines call it **irse a la B**, going down to the B. Even giants fall.

pages.prompt: Four of the big five clubs have been relegated. Which one never has?
pages.explain: Boca has never gone down. Their fans never let anyone forget it.

pages.text: River's drop in 2011 was probably the biggest shock in Argentine football history. More than ten years later, Boca fans still sing about it.

pages.prompt: Your team finished fifth this season, but your friend is still scared of going down. How is that possible?
options: Bad seasons from years ago still count
The top five teams swap leagues
The VAR can take points away
pages.explain: Relegation often uses the **promedio**, explained next.

pages.text: The **promedio** is your points per match over the last three seasons. One great year can't save a small club, and one bad year rarely sinks a big one. Critics say that's the point.
Every close call goes to **el VAR**, and the debate lasts until Thursday: **¿fue penal?** Was it a penalty? Old-timers still yell **orsai**: offside, the way their grandparents said it.

classes.title: Diego, 1986 and the pioneers
classes.summary: A World Cup with a shadow, a church for Diego, and the women who beat England first

pages.text: When **la Selección** plays, the country stops. Boca and River fans hug when Argentina scores. Three World Cups so far: 1978, 1986 and 2022.
1978 was won at home, under a military dictatorship that used the cup as propaganda. Many Argentines still feel uneasy celebrating it. If it comes up, listen more than you talk.
**Diego Maradona** grew up poor in Villa Fiorito and became the country's biggest idol. His face is painted on walls all over Buenos Aires.

pages.prompt: Some fans founded a “church” for Maradona. When do they celebrate Christmas?
options: June 22, the day he beat England
pages.explain: The **Iglesia Maradoniana** counts its years from his birth, in 1960. Half joke, half not.

pages.text: Mexico 1986, against England, four years after the **Malvinas** war. Diego scores with his hand, **la Mano de Dios**, then dribbles past half their team for the Goal of the Century.

pages.prompt: Diego wasn't the first Argentine to beat England at that same stadium. Who was?
pages.explain: In 1971, at an unofficial women's World Cup, Argentina's women beat England 4–1 at the Azteca.

pages.text: **Elba Selva** scored all four goals that day. August 21 is now the **Día de la Futbolista**, the Day of the Woman Footballer.

classes.title: Messi and Qatar
classes.summary: Heartbreak in Brazil, glory in Qatar

pages.text: **Messi** grew up in Rosario and left for Barcelona at 13. For years, some Argentines grumbled that he only shone for Barça.

pages.prompt: Why did Messi move to Barcelona as a kid?
options: Barça paid for his growth treatment
His dad got a job in Spain
He won a TV talent contest
pages.explain: He needed growth-hormone treatment his family couldn't afford. Barcelona paid for it.

pages.text: 2014 World Cup final, in Brazil: Germany scores in extra time. Messi walks past the trophy he couldn't touch. That photo still hurts.
After more lost finals, Messi quit the national team in 2016. Half the country begged him to come back. He did.
Qatar 2022, the final against France: 2–0, 2–2, 3–2, 3–3. Then penalties. **Dibu Martínez** saves one, **Montiel** scores the last. Messi finally lifts the cup.

pages.prompt: How many people filled Buenos Aires to welcome the team home?
pages.explain: Millions. The team bus couldn't get through, and the players finished the parade by helicopter.

pages.text: The soundtrack of Qatar: **“Muchachos, ahora nos volvimos a ilusionar”**, a fan chant sung to a song by La Mosca. Start it at any party and the whole room joins in.

classes.title: Beyond Buenos Aires
classes.summary: Rosario, Córdoba and La Plata, where the local derby beats Boca-River

pages.text: Outside the capital, the local **clásico** beats Boca–River. Ask someone from Rosario about Boca and River: a shrug. Ask about Newell's and Central: cancel your plans.

pages.prompt: Newell's fans are proudly called **leprosos**, lepers. Where does that come from?
options: They agreed to a charity match for leprosy patients
Their first stadium was an old hospital
pages.explain: The story goes: around 1920, both Rosario clubs were invited to play a charity match for leprosy patients. Newell's said yes.

pages.text: Legend says Rosario Central turned that match down, so they became the **canallas**: the scoundrels. Nobody can prove it, and both clubs wear the insults with pride.
Even the Selección splits: **Messi** grew up a Newell's kid, **Di María** is pure Central.
In La Plata it's **Estudiantes** against **Gimnasia**. Estudiantes fans are **pinchas**, Gimnasia fans are **triperos**. In Córdoba, it's **Belgrano** against **Talleres**.

pages.prompt: Gimnasia fans are called **triperos**, tripe people. Why?
options: Many early fans worked in meatpacking plants
They grill tripe outside every match
Their old shirt looked like tripe
pages.explain: The meatpacking plants near La Plata employed thousands. Their workers followed Gimnasia.

sections.title: Tango
sections.summary: The sad, sexy music of the Río de la Plata, and how not to embarrass yourself at a milonga

classes.title: Born on the edge of town
classes.summary: Two cities, one port, and a German squeezebox

pages.text: Tango was born in the late 1800s in the **arrabal**, the rough edge of town: tenements, corner bars, the port. The music of immigrants, sailors and workers.

pages.prompt: Polite Buenos Aires society found tango scandalous. What finally changed their minds?
options: A president danced it in public
It became a craze in Paris
The Church gave it its blessing
pages.explain: Once Paris loved it, the rich loved it too. Nothing like European approval to change a porteño's mind.

pages.text: Around 1900, men far outnumbered women in the city. So men often practiced tango with each other until they were good enough to dance with a woman.

pages.prompt: The most famous tango ever, **La Cumparsita**, was written where?
pages.explain: Gerardo Matos Rodríguez, a young Uruguayan, wrote it, and it premiered in a Montevideo café.

pages.text: So tango isn't only Argentine. It's **rioplatense**, from both sides of the river. In 2009 UNESCO listed it as heritage of both countries, and Uruguayans will remind you.
The sound of tango is the **bandoneón**, and it's German. The story goes it was meant for small churches with no organ. Hymns to tango bars in one boat trip.

pages.prompt: Why is the bandoneón famously hard to play?
options: Each button plays two different notes
It's as heavy as a small piano
It only plays in a single key
pages.explain: The note changes depending on whether the bellows open or close. Tangueros call it **el fueye**: the bellows.

pages.text: Early tango was quick and playful, played on flute, violin and guitar. Many say the bandoneón slowed it down, and that's where tango got its famous sadness.

classes.title: At the milonga
classes.summary: The unwritten rules of the dance floor

pages.text: A **milonga** is a tango dance night: tables around a wooden floor, a DJ or a live orquesta, every age dancing until late. Buenos Aires has one every night of the week.

pages.prompt: At a traditional milonga, how do you ask someone to dance?
options: Walk to their table and offer your hand
Catch their eye across the room and nod
Ask the DJ to dedicate them a song
pages.explain: That's the **cabeceo**: a look, a small nod. If they nod back, you go get them.

pages.text: And if they look away? That's a no, and nobody got rejected in public. That's the whole point of the cabeceo.
Music comes in **tandas**, sets of 3 or 4 songs. Then a short non-tango **cortina** plays, the floor clears, and everyone changes partners.

pages.prompt: Your partner says **“gracias”** after the first song. What just happened?
pages.explain: **Gracias** mid-tanda means “thanks, that's enough”. Want to keep going? Just smile and wait for the next song.

pages.text: Couples move counterclockwise in a **ronda**, like cars on a track. No passing, no big kicks, and never teach your partner on the floor.
The dinner shows with flying legs and a rose in someone's mouth? Porteños call that **tango for export**. At a milonga, the dance is small, close and improvised.

classes.title: Gardel
classes.summary: The voice, the smile, and the question of where he was born

pages.text: **Carlos Gardel** is *the* tango singer, and Argentina's first pop idol. Slicked-back hair, a movie-star smile, a voice people still call perfect.

pages.prompt: So where was Gardel born?
pages.explain: Most researchers say **Toulouse**. But Gardel once signed papers saying **Tacuarembó**, Uruguay, and many Uruguayans still claim him.

pages.text: Argentines settle it simply: he grew up in **Abasto**, the market barrio, so he's porteño. They call him **el Morocho del Abasto**.
In 1935, at the peak of his fame, Gardel died in a plane crash in **Medellín**, Colombia, while on tour. The whole country went into mourning.

pages.prompt: At his tomb in Chacarita cemetery, what do fans leave in his bronze statue's hand?
options: A folded page of sheet music
pages.explain: A lit **pucho**. Legend says if it burns all the way down, your wish comes true.

pages.text: His fans' favorite line: **cada día canta mejor**, he sings better every day. Dead since 1935, and still improving.
Friend whining about an ex for an hour? **Andá a cantarle a Gardel**: go sing it to Gardel. Cheeky, not rude.

classes.title: Big bands and a rebel
classes.summary: The golden age of the orquestas, and the rebel who broke the rules

pages.text: In the **1940s**, tango was pop music. Every club and radio station had an **orquesta típica**, and people followed bandleaders like football teams.
Tango DJs still build whole nights around them: **D'Arienzo**, punchy and rhythmic. **Di Sarli**, smooth and elegant. **Pugliese**, dark and dramatic.

pages.prompt: Pugliese was a communist and was jailed more than once. What did his orquesta do while he was inside?
options: Cancelled every show until he was freed
Played on, with a red carnation on his piano
Hired a new pianist and never looked back
pages.explain: A **clavel rojo** on the empty piano. Everyone in the room got the message.

pages.text: Then came the rebel: **Astor Piazzolla**. He grew up in New York, where his dad gave him a bandoneón as a kid.

pages.prompt: At 13, Piazzolla played in a Gardel film in New York, and Gardel invited him on his 1935 tour. What happened?
options: His father said he was too young
He joined and played every show
He said no to keep studying piano
pages.explain: Lucky boy. That was Gardel's last tour: it ended in the plane crash in Medellín.

pages.text: Back in Buenos Aires he played in **Troilo**'s orquesta, then studied classical music in Paris with **Nadia Boulanger**. She told him to stop hiding his tango.
So he mixed tango with jazz and classical: **tango nuevo**. Think **Libertango** and **Adiós Nonino**.
Traditionalists called him **el asesino del tango**, and **“eso no es tango”** followed him for years. Today he's among the most played Argentine composers in the world.

classes.title: What tango sings about
classes.summary: Mom, the barrio, the woman who left, and a world gone wrong

pages.text: Tango lyrics have favorite subjects: the woman who left (always her fault), mom (a saint), the old barrio, and nostalgia for everything.
Tango poet **Discépolo** summed it up: **el tango es un pensamiento triste que se baila**. A sad thought you can dance to.

pages.prompt: Gardel's **Volver** has tango's most quoted line. What does it claim?
pages.explain: **“Que veinte años no es nada.”** Heard at reunions and birthdays, anywhere time has passed and everyone pretends it hasn't.

pages.text: **Mi Buenos Aires querido** is a man far away, dreaming of coming home. Ask any Argentine living abroad whether it makes them cry.
**Cambalache**, also by Discépolo, isn't about love. It says the world is a junk shop where a donkey and a great professor count the same.

pages.prompt: What happened to **Cambalache** in the 1940s?
options: It was banned from the radio
It won a national music prize
pages.explain: The military government of the 1940s banned it, along with lots of lunfardo. Being banned only made it more famous. It still sounds like this morning's news.

pages.text: Its name stuck, too. When something is a total, unfair mess, Argentines sigh: **“esto es un cambalache.”**

sections.title: Música
sections.summary: Rock nacional, folklore, cumbia, trap, and crowds louder than the band

classes.title: Rock nacional
classes.summary: Rock in Spanish, born in a café bathroom and raised under a dictatorship

pages.text: Before 1967, rock here meant copies: foreign hits, translated or sung in English. Then **Los Gatos** released **“La balsa”**, an original song in Spanish, and it sold. **Rock nacional** was born.

pages.prompt: The story goes that “La balsa” was finished somewhere unusual. Where?
options: In a café bathroom, hiding from the waiters
In a police cell, after a noisy night out
On a ferry crossing the Río de la Plata
pages.explain: The bathroom of **La Perla del Once**, a 24-hour café whose waiters kept kicking loud musicians out. At least, that's the legend.

pages.text: Two names you must know. **Luis Alberto Spinetta**, **el Flaco**, wrote dreamy, poetic songs. **Charly García** became the wild genius: brilliant, unpredictable, loved.

pages.prompt: Charly once made a famous exit from a ninth-floor hotel room in Mendoza. How?
options: He jumped out the window into the pool
He climbed down on knotted bedsheets
He slid down the laundry chute
pages.explain: Ninth floor, into the pool, and he walked away. People tell Charly stories like this with pure affection.

pages.text: Under the 1976–83 dictatorship, rock was censored and harassed, so musicians sang in metaphors. For many kids, a concert was the only place they could feel free together.

pages.prompt: Then came the 1982 Malvinas war against Britain. What happened to Argentine rock on the radio?
options: It took over, because English songs were pulled
It was banned completely until the war ended
pages.explain: The regime that harassed rockers suddenly needed Spanish songs to fill the airwaves. Bands went from underground to mainstream almost overnight.

pages.text: **Soda Stereo** took Argentine rock across Latin America. At their farewell show, **Gustavo Cerati** closed with **“¡Gracias… totales!”** People still say it to thank someone big time.

classes.title: Folklore, peñas and pañuelos
classes.summary: Guitars, handkerchiefs and the voice of La Negra

pages.text: In Argentina **folklore** isn't museum music. It's the living sound of the provinces: guitars, violins and the **bombo legüero**, a deep drum of wood and hide.
Its rhythms have names, like **zamba**, **chacarera** and **chamamé**. Young people still sing them at parties, especially in the north.
**Mercedes Sosa**, from Tucumán, was **La Negra**, a nickname said with love. Her **“Gracias a la vida”** still makes whole rooms cry.

pages.prompt: During the dictatorship, where was Mercedes Sosa arrested?
options: On stage, in the middle of a concert
At the airport, back from a tour
At home, while writing a song
pages.explain: Arrested mid-concert, she went into exile in Europe. When she came back, still under the dictatorship, she packed theater after theater.

pages.text: A **peña** is a folklore night: long tables, **empanadas**, wine and live music. There's no audience. When a chacarera starts, people dance between the tables, then sit down and keep eating.

pages.prompt: The **zamba** is a slow dance for couples, with a white handkerchief. How do they use it?
options: They wave it while circling, never touching
They tie it around their partner's wrist
They drop it for the other to pick up
pages.explain: The **pañuelo** turns the zamba into slow flirting. And no, it's not the Brazilian samba. The fast one, with stomping and finger snaps, is the **chacarera**.

pages.text: Every January, the small town of **Cosquín**, in the Córdoba hills, hosts the national folk festival: nine nights, **las nueve lunas**. Each night opens with a shout: **“¡Aquí Cosquín!”**
Invited to dance at a peña? Say **“¡Dale!”** and get up. Nobody expects a foreigner to dance well. Getting up is what counts.

classes.title: Cumbia and cuarteto
classes.summary: The bailanta, a cumbia saint, and the tunga tunga from Córdoba

pages.text: Rock fills stadiums, but **cumbia** fills the dance floor. Born in Colombia, it became deeply Argentine in the dance halls of the suburbs: the **bailantas**.
At every wedding the DJ eventually puts on cumbia, and even your serious uncle turns out to be a **cumbiero**. You don't have to like it. You just have to dance.

pages.prompt: **Gilda** became one of the biggest cumbia stars of the 90s. What was her job before?
pages.explain: She became a star in her 30s, in a scene run by men.

pages.text: In 1996 Gilda's tour bus crashed on **Ruta 12**. People began asking her for miracles at a shrine by the road. The Church never made her a saint. The people did.
In the late 90s, with the economy collapsing, a rawer style grew in the poorest neighborhoods: **cumbia villera**. Critics hear crude lyrics. Fans hear the honest voice of the barrio.
In **Córdoba** the party sound is **cuarteto**, with a bouncy piano beat everyone calls **tunga tunga**. Its king, **La Mona Jiménez**, has played packed dances for decades.

pages.prompt: Cuarteto recently got an honor that tango got back in 2009. Which one?
options: A place on UNESCO's heritage list
A national day off in its name
pages.explain: UNESCO added cuarteto to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage. Not bad for music born in Córdoba's dance halls.

pages.text: **Rodrigo**, **el Potro**, took cuarteto to Buenos Aires and filled the Luna Park again and again. He died young, in a car crash after a show, and his songs still close every party.

classes.title: Trap, RKT and Bizarrap
classes.summary: From freestyle battles in a park to the biggest stages in the world

pages.text: Argentine trap fills stadiums now. Its big names, like **Duki**, **Trueno** and **Wos**, didn't come from music schools or record labels.

pages.prompt: So where did they learn?
options: Rap battles on the steps of a park
Singing in church choirs as kids
Busking for coins on the subte
pages.explain: For years, kids met on the steps of **Parque Rivadavia** for **El Quinto Escalón**: free freestyle battles, and the crowd shouted for the winner.

pages.text: **Bizarrap** is a producer who hides behind a cap and dark glasses. In his **BZRP Music Sessions**, one guest raps or sings over his beat in a tiny studio.

pages.prompt: Before producing, how did Bizarrap get known on YouTube?
pages.explain: He cut and posted clips of battles like the Quinto Escalón. The scene that made Duki and Trueno made him too.

pages.text: A Biza **sesión** can launch a career overnight. In 2023 his session with **Shakira**, a song aimed at her ex, broke YouTube records.
Women run the charts too: **María Becerra** sold out River's stadium, **Tini** went from Disney star to pop queen, and **Nicki Nicole** broke out of Rosario.

pages.prompt: The newest party sound is **RKT**. Where does the name come from?
pages.explain: DJs at **Rescate**, a club in San Martín, just outside the city, started mixing it in the 2000s, labeling the files “RKT”.

pages.text: RKT is reggaetón plus cumbia villera, with huge bass. **L-Gante** made it explode, recording his first hits on a laptop the government gave out to schoolkids.

classes.title: Live: pogo, bengalas and misas
classes.summary: Why foreign bands leave Argentina a little shaken

pages.text: At a **recital** here, the crowd doesn't just listen. It sings every word, often louder than the band. Foreign artists leave a little shaken.

pages.prompt: The Rolling Stones named a whole documentary after something Latin American crowds do. What?
options: The way fans camp out for days
The flares they light in the stands
pages.explain: *Olé, Olé, Olé!* Between songs, the stadium sings it football style, followed by the artist's name: **“Olé, olé, olé, olé… Charly, Charly!”**

pages.text: Argentina has so many Stones fans they have a name: **rollingas**. And when a band walks off before the encore, the whole stadium shouts **“¡Otro, otro!”**
**Los Redondos** barely talked to the press, yet fans crossed the country to see them. They didn't call the shows concerts. They called them **misas**: masses.

pages.prompt: Near the stage, hundreds of people jump and crash into each other: the **pogo**. What happens if someone falls?
options: The people closest pick them up
pages.explain: It looks like chaos, but it has a code: **si alguien se cae, se lo levanta**. Whoever falls gets picked up.

pages.text: In the 90s, barrio rock crowds, **rock chabón**, brought the football stadium to gigs: banners, chants and **bengalas**, flares lit right in the crowd.
The flares had a dark side. At a show at **República Cromañón**, a flare set the ceiling on fire. The club was overcrowded, an exit was locked. **194 people died**, most of them young.
It changed live music forever: much stricter rules, and a flare indoors is now unthinkable. Every December 30, families still gather to remember.

sections.title: Cómo hablamos
sections.summary: Vos, the “sh” sound, lunfardo and a lot of hands

classes.title: Vos, not tú
classes.summary: The little pronoun that makes you sound Argentine

pages.text: Your textbook taught you **tú**. Forget it here. Argentines say **vos**: **vos sos**, **vos tenés**, **¿vos querés?** Say “tú tienes” and people understand you, then clock you as a textbook learner.
Why vos? It's old Spanish. The usual story: **tú** took over in the rich colonial capitals, Lima and Mexico City. The Río de la Plata was a poor, far-off corner, and nobody updated it.

pages.prompt: So what did Argentine schools teach kids for decades?
options: Tú, which nobody said at home
pages.explain: Grammar books kept pushing **tú**. Only in 1982 did the Academia Argentina de Letras accept vos as correct, educated Spanish.

pages.text: Plural “you” is always **ustedes**. **Vosotros** is for Spain. Here it survives mainly in the national anthem, which opens with **“Oíd, mortales”**.

pages.prompt: In Buenos Aires, who usually gets the formal **usted**?
pages.explain: The waiter, your doctor, often even your friend's grandma: **vos**. Some people still use usted with the very old, but vos is the normal default.

pages.text: So politeness lives in the tone: **disculpá**, **¿me podrías…?**, **por favor**. A warm vos beats a stiff usted every time.
You don't even need to say vos. The ending does the work: **¿Tenés cambio?** is the whole sentence. Short, friendly, local.

classes.title: Sho, che and the melody
classes.summary: The sound, the word and the tune that give a porteño away

pages.text: The quickest way to spot a porteño: **y** and **ll** sound like “sh”. **Yo** is “sho”, **calle** is “cashe”, **me llamo** is “me shamo”.

pages.prompt: A Buenos Aires grandma and her granddaughter both say **yo**. What's different?
options: Nothing: the sound hasn't changed in a century
Grandma says “yo”, just like in Madrid
pages.explain: The older sound is a buzzing **zh**, like the s in *measure*. Younger porteños, led by women, pushed it to a crisp **sh**. Both are 100% porteño.

pages.text: The sh isn't only Argentine, it's **rioplatense**: Montevideo says it too. And not all of Argentina does. Parts of the north and northeast keep a softer y.

pages.prompt: Researchers compared the melody of Buenos Aires Spanish with other ways of speaking. Which was it closest to?
pages.explain: Closer to **Naples** than to Madrid. That's why foreigners say porteños sound a bit Italian.

pages.text: The tune most likely arrived with the huge wave of Italian immigrants around 1900. Their accents faded, but the melody stuck.
Then there's **che**: hey, dude, listen. Nobody knows where it comes from. Guaraní? Mapudungun? Valencian? Pick a theory and defend it over a mate.

pages.prompt: Ernesto Guevara became world-famous as “Che”. Who gave him the nickname?
options: His Cuban comrades, because he said it constantly
His mother, who called him that as a baby
The press, after his first speech in Havana
pages.explain: To the Cubans, **che** was the most Argentine thing about him. It became his name.

pages.text: End a story with **¿viste?**, “you know?”, and you'll sound local instantly: **Hacía un frío, ¿viste?**

classes.title: Lunfardo
classes.summary: The street slang born in the conventillos

pages.text: Around 1900, Buenos Aires was packed with immigrants, mostly Italians and Spaniards, crammed into tenements called **conventillos**. Out of that mix came **lunfardo**, the city's street slang.

pages.prompt: Who were the first people to write lunfardo down, in the late 1800s?
options: Police, who thought it was a thieves' code
Teachers, trying to stamp it out
pages.explain: Police officers and criminologists. Then it turned out bakers, clerks and grandmas talked like that too.

pages.text: Then **tango** carried it onto the radio, and lunfardo went from the tenement patio to every living room in the country.
It's no museum piece. Everyone, from teenagers to bank managers, says **me voy al laburo**, I'm off to work. From Italian *lavoro*.

pages.prompt: The city bus is the **bondi**. Where does the word come from, the story goes?
options: The name of an Italian bus company
A Guaraní word for a big box
pages.explain: Brazilians called trams **bonde**, supposedly after the bonds sold as tickets. Buenos Aires borrowed it, and when the trams vanished, the name jumped onto the bus.

pages.text: **Chamuyo** is smooth talk: half truth, all charm. You chamuyás a date, a cop, your boss. And when a story sounds too good: **eso es puro chamuyo**.
One to hear, not say: **mina**, for a woman. Everyone uses it, but it's a bit macho, and from a foreigner it can land badly.
Slang has its own academy here: the **Academia Porteña del Lunfardo**, founded in 1962. Scholars meet to study street words the way others study Cervantes.

classes.title: Vesre, re and posta
classes.summary: Words backwards, words turned up, and the truth

pages.text: Porteños love flipping words. Swap the syllables of **revés**, backwards, and you get **vesre**: the name of the game, played on itself.

pages.prompt: Flipped words sound like a party game, but one of these is completely everyday. Which?
pages.explain: **¿Quién garpa?**, who's paying?, ends plenty of dinners. **Gotán** and **dorima** mostly live in old tangos.

pages.text: Another flip you'll hear constantly: **hotel** becomes **telo**. Remember that one. It matters.

pages.prompt: At a party you say you're staying at “un telo re lindo en Palermo”. Everyone bursts out laughing. Why?
options: A telo is a hotel rented by the hour
Telo is slang for a cheap hostel
Telo is what little kids call a hotel
pages.explain: A **telo** is a love hotel: rooms by the hour, discreet entrance. Great story for the rest of the night, though.

pages.text: Plenty of people live with their parents well into their twenties, so telos are a normal, even cheerful, part of city life. For your stay, just say **hotel**.
Want “very”? Put **re** in front: **re lindo**, **re lejos**. It even works alone: **—¿Te gustó? —¡Re!**
**Posta** means “for real”. **¿Posta?** is “Seriously?”, and **la posta** is the real story. Now you know why this app is called Posta.

classes.title: Hands and texts
classes.summary: Gestures you'll see and shortcuts you'll read

pages.text: Porteños don't just talk, they perform. Watch two friends argue about football across the street and you'll get the gist without hearing a word.

pages.prompt: Someone cuts in the bus line. A lady pinches her fingertips together, pointing up, and bobs her wrist. What's she saying?
pages.explain: That's the **montoncito**: **¿qué te pasa?** From friendly to threatening, depending on the face. It even has its own emoji: 🤌.

pages.text: Two more you'll see daily. Flat hand rocking side to side: **más o menos**. Finger pulling down your lower eyelid: careful, **¡ojo!** Add a shrug and you'll survive a whole conversation.
Argentines love **audios**: WhatsApp voice notes instead of typing. A three-minute audio just to say you're running late? Completely normal.
When they do type, nobody writes a full sentence if a few letters will do. **tqm**, te quiero mucho, closes half the chats in the country.

pages.prompt: You suggest a 7 a.m. Sunday run. Your friend replies: **“bue”**. How excited are they?
pages.explain: **Bue** is **bueno** with a sigh: fine, if we must. Expect them to show up late.

pages.text: **Nada que ver** is the all-purpose “not at all”: **—¿Estás enojado? —No, nada que ver.**

sections.title: Dichos y refranes
sections.summary: Expressions, idioms and sayings: how Argentines really talk

classes.title: Everyday expressions
classes.summary: The phrases you'll hear before lunch on any given day

pages.text: Exam tomorrow, nothing studied? **Estoy al horno**: I'm in the oven. Completely doomed? **Al horno con papas**: in the oven, with potatoes, like a Sunday roast.

pages.prompt: When you finally get something, you say **“me cayó la ficha”**: the ficha dropped. What was the ficha?
options: A token for old pay phones
A tile in a game of dominoes
A chip at the casino table
pages.explain: Old public phones ran on **fichas**. The call only went through when the token dropped. Now it's the moment the penny drops.

pages.text: Your roommate hasn't left the couch all week, and exams start Monday. Time to tell him: **“Ponete las pilas.”** Put your batteries in. Get going.
A cancelled plan, rain on a Saturday, a two-hour line at the bank. You sigh: **“¡Qué garrón!”** What a drag.

pages.prompt: You didn't study, so in the exam you write a full page of confident nonsense. What do Argentines say you did?
options: **Pateaste el tablero**: you kicked the board
**Tiraste la toalla**: you threw in the towel
pages.explain: **Mandar fruta** is winging it with words. Students do it in exams, and plenty of politicians do it on TV.

pages.text: Your friend has to go to a boring wedding alone, so you go with her. You **le hacés la gamba**: you lend her your leg. It means keeping someone company when it counts.
The best thing you can say about someone is simple: **es re buena onda**. Easygoing, warm, good vibes. The coworker who never says hi? **Mala onda**.

classes.title: Más contento que perro con dos colas
classes.summary: The comparisons Argentines use to exaggerate everything

pages.text: Why say “very happy” when you can be **más contento que perro con dos colas**? Happier than a dog with two tails. Argentines love a good **más … que**.
The line at the bank, a meeting, the last week before payday. Anything endless is **más largo que esperanza de pobre**: longer than a poor man's hope.

pages.prompt: A guy at the party has explained his crypto plan to you three times. Your friend whispers: **“Es más pesado que un collar de…”** Heavier than a necklace of what?
pages.explain: **Más pesado que collar de melones.** **Pesado** is heavy, and also a pain. Picture wearing melons around your neck all night.

pages.text: Fake stuff is **trucho**. And nothing's faker than a bill that doesn't exist: **más trucho que billete de tres pesos**. That street-stall “original” Messi shirt? Exactly that.
The friend who can't just pick a restaurant **tiene más vueltas que una calesita**: more turns than a merry-go-round.

pages.prompt: Your friend's ex walks into the bar like he owns it. You whisper: **“Se cree la última … del desierto.”** He thinks he's the last what in the desert?
pages.explain: **La última Coca-Cola del desierto**: the one thing everybody wants. Or so he thinks.

pages.text: And a class that won't end, or a film where nothing happens? **Más aburrido que chupar un clavo**: more boring than sucking a nail.

classes.title: Grandma's refranes
classes.summary: The old sayings every abuela has ready for any occasion

pages.text: A **refrán** is an old proverb, and most came from Spain. What's Argentine is the timing: your abuela has one ready before you finish telling her the problem.
And she only says half. You complain about your aunt's ugly sweater: **“Y bueno, a caballo regalado…”** Everyone knows the rest: **no se le miran los dientes**. Don't look a gift horse in the mouth.

pages.prompt: After a bad breakup, your friend won't even go on a date. Abuela nods: **“El que se quema con leche, ve una vaca y…”** Burned by milk, you see a cow and…?
pages.explain: You cry at the sight of a cow. Once hurt, you fear anything that looks like it.

pages.text: New friends look a bit shady? Abuela raises an eyebrow: **“Decime con quién andás y te diré quién sos.”** Tell me who you hang out with, and I'll tell you who you are.
Your friend swears, again, that he starts the gym on Monday. **Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho**: from saying to doing, it's a long way.

pages.prompt: In English, a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. In Spanish, it's worth how many flying?
pages.explain: **Más vale pájaro en mano que cien volando.** Same lesson, much bigger flock.

pages.text: And when something goes wrong, the silver-lining one: **no hay mal que por bien no venga**. There's no bad thing that doesn't bring something good.

classes.title: Argentine philosophy in six sentences
classes.summary: The maxims that explain how the country sees itself

pages.text: Crisis after crisis, Argentines built a set of sayings that are part shrug, part joke, part survival guide. Hear them and you'll get how people here think.
The bank ignores your complaint? Call every day and make noise. **El que no llora no mama**: the baby who doesn't cry doesn't get fed.

pages.prompt: A new tax is announced. By dinnertime, your friends already know three ways around it. They shrug: **“Hecha la ley, hecha la…”** Made the law, made the what?
pages.explain: As soon as a law is made, so is the trick around it. Said with a shrug about bureaucracy, taxes and life.

pages.text: Skipping the line, dodging the fare, finding the loophole: that's **viveza criolla**. The one who pulls it off is a **vivo**. The one who plays fair risks being called a **gil**, a sucker.

pages.prompt: With all that viveza, what do porteños do at a bus stop?
options: Stand in a neat single-file line
Crowd the door, first come first in
Let the oldest board, then push
pages.explain: The **fila del colectivo** is sacred. Visitors are often amazed. Cutting it is the kind of viveza nobody forgives.

pages.text: The fridge door shut with a belt, a car that runs on a prayer, sometimes the whole economy: **atado con alambre**. Held together with wire.
A goal in the 94th minute, a flight you caught by seconds. When luck saves the day, someone will say it: **Dios es argentino**. God is Argentine.
And for a friend going through hard times, the kindest one: **siempre que llovió, paró**. Every time it rained, it stopped.

sections.title: Puteadas
sections.summary: Argentine swearing: what it means, and when to keep your mouth shut

classes.title: Boludo, the word that does everything
classes.summary: Greeting, insult, punctuation: one word, many jobs

pages.text: A **puteada** is a swear or an insult. Argentines swear a lot, and often with love. The goal here: understand them, and know when to keep quiet.

pages.prompt: First week at a new job. A coworker your age says: **“Che, boludo, ¿venís a almorzar?”** What does it tell you?
options: He thinks you messed something up
He's already treating you as a friend
He's testing whether you'll push back
pages.explain: Between people who get along, **boludo** is closer to “dude” than to “idiot”. Here's how that happened.

pages.text: **Boludo** literally means big-balled: an idiot. But between friends it softened into “dude”. **¿Qué hacés, boludo?** is just “What's up, man?”
Some porteños use it like a comma: **“Fui al súper, boludo, y no había nada, boludo.”**
Same word, said slowly with a stare, is still an insult. From a local friend it's warm. From a stranger with an accent, it can land like a slap.

pages.prompt: Boludo has a longer cousin: **pelotudo**. Compared with boludo, how does it land?
pages.explain: **Boludo** can be love. **Pelotudo** rarely is.

pages.text: **¡Qué pelotudo!** means “What an idiot!”, and it's meant. Understand it, never say it.
Say boludo only once your friends say it to you. Never to a waiter, a driver or someone you just met.

classes.title: Gil, forro, chanta: the cast of characters
classes.summary: The people Argentines love to complain about

pages.text: Argentines love complaining about certain kinds of people, and each kind has a name. Meet the cast.

pages.prompt: A taxi driver charges you triple because you're a tourist, and you pay. What does your Argentine friend call you, lovingly?
pages.explain: You got fooled, so you're the **gil**: the sucker. **No seas gil** means don't be a sucker.

pages.text: It's old tango slang: the gil got scammed, the **vivo** did the scamming. Rude, but mild enough to tease friends with.
The **chanta** is all talk: brags, promises, never delivers. The plumber who says **“mañana vengo”** for three weeks? Chanta.

pages.prompt: Of these three, which one hurts most when said to someone's face?
pages.explain: **Forro**, by far. Here's why.

pages.text: **Forro** means lining, and it's slang for condom. Said to a person, it means mean or disloyal. It's about character, not brains. Understand it, never say it.
The friend who won't stop bugging you is a **rompebolas**: a ball-breaker. Between friends it's a jokey complaint, not a war.
With a stranger, none of these. When in doubt, laugh and keep quiet: you'll sound more local than any puteada.

classes.title: La puta madre: pure frustration
classes.summary: The exclamations for when everything goes wrong

pages.text: Stub your toe, miss the bus, see the inflation numbers: **¡La puta madre!** Nobody's mother is involved. It's just “damn it!”, aimed at the universe.
It comes in levels: **la puta que lo parió**, then the maximum, **la re puta que lo parió**. Or just a long, tired **“la puta…”**

pages.prompt: You tell your friend you met Messi at the airport. She laughs: **“¡Andá a cagar!”**, literally “go take a shit”. What does she mean?
pages.explain: Laughing plus big news means disbelief. Said cold, with a door closing, the same words mean “get lost”.

pages.text: **La concha de tu madre** is the heavy one, very vulgar. Shouted at nobody after your phone hits the floor, it's frustration. Aimed at a person, it's a serious insult.
**Me chupa un huevo** (egg = testicle) means “I couldn't care less”. Really don't care? **Me chupa un huevo y la mitad del otro.**

pages.prompt: Around kids and grandmas, Argentines swap **mierda** for a harmless word that sounds similar. Which one?
pages.explain: **¡Miércoles!** Wednesday. Everyone knows what you meant, and nobody's offended.

pages.text: Same trick for la puta: **¡la pucha!** Safe with kids, bosses and grandmas, and it still sounds like you mean it.

classes.title: Reading the room
classes.summary: The stadium, the traffic, and your partner's grandma

pages.text: At **la cancha**, swearing is a sport. The referee hears **“¡Cobrá, referí!”** plus a few mothers. Some fans joke it's part of the ticket price.
Careful with the chants, though. Many carry slurs about gay people or other nationalities, and the pushback is growing. Clap and jump; the words can wait.

pages.prompt: In Qatar, shy, polite Messi snapped at a Dutch player on live TV: **“¿Qué mirás, bobo?”** What happened next?
options: It ended up on T-shirts and mugs
FIFA banned him for a match
pages.explain: **Bobo** is mild, almost childish, which made it even funnier. Within days it was a national catchphrase.

pages.text: Buenos Aires traffic turns saints into sailors. Green light, one second: **¡Dale, boludo!** Cut off: **¿Quién te dio el registro?**, who gave you a license? Usually it's just venting.
Before you swear, ask: would I say this in front of my partner's grandma? With close friends, go ahead. With your boss, a cop or a stranger, keep it clean.

pages.prompt: In 2009, right after qualifying for the World Cup, coach Maradona told journalists on live TV: **“que la chupen”**, suck it. What happened?
options: FIFA banned him for two months
He was fired the next week
pages.explain: FIFA suspended him and fined him. Argentines, meanwhile, turned the line into a classic.

pages.text: Swearing badly makes you sound rude. Swearing well makes you sound local. It's all in the timing.

sections.title: Costumbres
sections.summary: Kisses, late arrivals, long goodbyes and a very full calendar

classes.title: Hello, with a kiss
classes.summary: One kiss, everybody, every time

pages.text: In Argentina you say hi with **un beso**: one kiss, cheek to cheek, lips to the air. Not two like in Spain. Just one, and quick.

pages.prompt: Two Argentine guys, old friends, meet at a bar. How do they say hi?
options: A quick nod and a smile
pages.explain: Often a kiss plus a pat on the back. Brothers, fathers and sons too. A handshake between friends would feel oddly stiff.

pages.text: Arrive at a party of twelve and you **saludás a todos**: you go around and kiss every single person, strangers included. A wave from the door feels cold.

pages.prompt: Your first week at a new job in Buenos Aires. How do your coworkers greet you in the morning?
pages.explain: In many offices it's a kiss, every morning, often even with the boss. Nobody thinks it's intimate. It's just hello.

pages.text: The exception: a very formal first meeting, like a job interview. Then it's often a handshake. Watch what the other person does. By the second meeting, it's usually a kiss.
Then comes **¿Todo bien?** or **¿Qué hacés?** Not real questions, just hello. **“Todo bien, ¿vos?”** is the whole answer. The long version comes later, over a mate.
Meeting someone new at a party? Lean in, kiss, and say your name: **“Hola, soy Sam.”** That's all anyone expects.

classes.title: Argentine time
classes.summary: Late arrivals, loose plans and goodbyes that never end

pages.text: Invited to dinner at someone's home **a las nueve**? Nobody expects you at nine. Twenty or thirty minutes late is normal. Arriving early is the real faux pas.
That's social life only. Work, classes and the doctor run on the clock. Be on time, or at least text.

pages.prompt: Your friend texts **“ya salgo”**: I'm leaving now. What's she most likely doing?
pages.explain: **Ya salgo** has padding built in, and **llego en cinco** means fifteen. Nobody's lying: everyone knows how to read it.

pages.text: Plans live in the WhatsApp group, and the key phrase is **vamos viendo**: let's see. The plan is alive, but nothing's fixed until an hour before.
Never show up empty-handed. The host will say **“no traigas nada”**, don't bring anything. Bring wine or dessert anyway.
