pages.prompt: You announce **“bueno, me voy yendo”**: well, I'm heading off. How long until you're out the door?
pages.explain: Another glass appears. Then a kiss for everyone. Then a chat at the door. Totally normal.

pages.text: Slipping out without goodbyes is **irse a la francesa**: leaving French-style. People notice, and they'll bring it up next time.

classes.title: Going out
classes.summary: The previa, the boliche and breakfast at sunrise

pages.text: The **boliche**, the nightclub, opens around one. The dancing really starts at two or three. Getting home at six, with the sun up, is a normal Saturday.

pages.prompt: Your friends say: “Previa at Tomi's, then the boliche.” You get to Tomi's at nine. What do you find?
options: The party already in full swing
pages.explain: At nine the night hasn't started. The previa gets going around midnight.

pages.text: **La previa** is drinks at a friend's place before going out: cheaper, your own music, and you can hear each other. For plenty of people it's the best part. The boliche is just the excuse.

pages.prompt: It's 4 a.m. and the boliche is packed. Which of these will you almost never hear?
pages.explain: Tango lives in the **milongas**, with their own crowd. The boliche runs on cumbia, reggaetón and whatever everyone can shout along to.

pages.text: And six a.m. isn't always the end. An **after** keeps the party going once the boliche closes.
Everyone else heads for **café con medialunas** as the cafés open, then bed until lunch.
Sunday afternoon exists mostly to recover: blinds down, a mate, and a group chat reconstructing what happened.

classes.title: No filter
classes.summary: Body comments, money talk, and the gauchada

pages.text: Your aunt sees you after the holidays: **“¡Estás más gordito!”** You've put on a bit of weight. She means it warmly, like “you look well fed.”
Couples call each other **gordo** and **gorda** as a pet name, whatever their size. It's the Argentine *honey*.

pages.prompt: A stranger on the street shouts **“¡Flaco!”** at you. Skinny! What does he want?
options: To say you look too thin today
To warn you about a pickpocket
pages.explain: **Flaco** is how you call out to a guy you don't know. **“¡Flaco, se te cayó esto!”** Hey, you dropped this.

pages.text: Younger people are more careful with body comments. Laugh off grandma's, but don't start making your own.

pages.prompt: Someone you met ten minutes ago asks how much you pay in rent. How should you take it?
options: As a sign she's flat hunting
pages.explain: After decades of inflation, prices are everyone's favorite topic. **¿Cuánto pagaste?** is fair game, for your phone, your shoes, your rent.

pages.text: One of the nicest questions in the language: **“¿Me hacés una gauchada?”** Can you do me a favor? A **gauchada** is a favor done for free, just because.
Lending your drill, a ride to the airport at dawn, a stranger helping push your stalled car: all gauchadas. Nobody keeps score.

classes.title: Christmas in summer
classes.summary: Cold vitel toné, fireworks at midnight, then the beach

pages.text: Christmas in Argentina falls in summer. It can be scorching, and Papá Noel still wears his wool coat.
The **arbolito** goes up on **8 December**, a public holiday. The big night isn't the 25th: it's **Nochebuena**, the 24th, with a long dinner, often outdoors.

pages.prompt: It's Nochebuena. What's the classic star of the table?
options: Veal in a creamy tuna sauce
pages.explain: **Vitel toné**, an Italian import, served cold. Plus **pan dulce**, **turrón** and **sidra**. And yes, often an asado too.

pages.text: At midnight everyone stands for the **brindis**, the toast. The sky explodes with fireworks from every backyard and balcony.

pages.prompt: When do most families open the presents?
pages.explain: Presents at midnight, with the fireworks still going. The 25th is for leftovers and naps.

pages.text: New Year's repeats the formula: dinner, toast, fireworks. Then the city empties. January is holiday month, and everyone who can heads for the beach.
On 6 January, kids leave their shoes out with grass and water for the camels of the **Reyes Magos**, the Three Kings.

classes.title: The calendar
classes.summary: Friends' Day, spring, long weekends and birthdays

pages.text: On **20 de julio** Argentina celebrates **Día del Amigo**, Friends' Day. Restaurants are packed and your phone won't stop buzzing: **“¡Feliz Día del Amigo!”**

pages.prompt: Why July 20?
options: It's the day humans first walked on the Moon
It's the birthday of a famous tango singer
It's the day Argentina's first club was founded
pages.explain: An Argentine, **Enrique Febbraro**, watched the Moon landing and thought the whole world should celebrate friendship that day.

pages.text: **21 de septiembre** is a double party: first day of spring and **Día del Estudiante**. Students fill the parks with picnics and guitars. Want a quiet walk? Not that day.
Argentines love a **finde largo**, a long weekend. Some years the government even adds a **feriado puente**: a bridge day off, just to join a holiday to the weekend.
The birthday song here is **“Que los cumplas feliz”**. Then your friends pull your ears: the **tirón de orejas**, one tug for each year.

pages.prompt: Your friend's birthday is tomorrow and you won't see her. When do you send your message?
pages.explain: Wishing **feliz cumple** early is **yeta**: bad luck. Even Pope Francis, a porteño, warned a crowd who greeted him early, before his 80th birthday.

pages.text: Set an alarm. A message right at midnight is the classic move: the first one wins.

sections.title: Buenos Aires
sections.summary: Barrios, bondis, cafés and the city that never goes to bed

classes.title: Porteños and everyone else
classes.summary: Capital, Provincia, el interior, and what they say about each other

pages.text: People from the city of Buenos Aires are **porteños**, people of the port. For centuries, ships, goods and millions of immigrants all came in through here.

pages.prompt: Is the city of Buenos Aires part of the Province of Buenos Aires?
options: No, the city is on its own
Only the southern half of it
pages.explain: The city, **CABA**, is its own district. The Provincia wraps around it, and its capital is a different city: **La Plata**.

pages.text: Cross the **General Paz** avenue and you're in the **conurbano**, a huge ring of suburbs where millions more live. People out there aren't porteños, and they call the city just **Capital**.
Porteños call everywhere outside the metro area **el interior**. People from Córdoba or Mendoza don't love it: it makes the whole country sound like a backyard.

pages.prompt: The provinces have a famous comeback: “God is everywhere…” How does it end?
options: “…but his office is in Buenos Aires”
pages.explain: **“Dios está en todas partes, pero atiende en Buenos Aires.”** Everything important gets decided in the capital, and everyone else has to go and ask.

pages.text: The stereotypes fly both ways. The provinces say porteños are **agrandados**, full of themselves, and talk too fast. Porteños joke that the provinces live slower. Both sides exaggerate, and both laugh.
Traveling around? Don't say you're touring “el interior”. Name the province: **“Estoy recorriendo Mendoza.”**

classes.title: A city of barrios
classes.summary: La Boca, San Telmo, Palermo and a cemetery full of legends

pages.text: Ask porteños where they're from and you'll get a barrio, not a city: Boedo, Flores, Palermo. Each has its own cafés, its own club and its own pride.
**La Boca** sits where the Riachuelo meets the river. Its dockworkers built houses of wood and **chapa**, painted, the story goes, with leftover paint from the shipyards.

pages.prompt: La Boca's famous colorful street, **Caminito**, is named after what?
pages.explain: The tango **“Caminito”**, by **Juan de Dios Filiberto**, a composer from La Boca itself.

pages.text: **San Telmo** is the old colonial south: cobblestones, balconies, antique shops. On Sundays, calle **Defensa** turns into a street market, with tango dancers on the corners.
**Palermo** is the biggest barrio, so people keep inventing sub-barrios: **Palermo Soho**, **Palermo Hollywood**, Palermo Chico. The joke: soon everything will be “Palermo something”.
In the **Recoleta Cemetery**, marble family vaults line the paths like little streets, with presidents, writers and lots of cats. Most visitors come for one grave: **Evita**'s.

pages.prompt: Another famous tomb there belongs to a young woman, Rufina Cambaceres. What's her legend?
pages.explain: The story goes that she woke up inside her coffin. Historians doubt it, but the legend always wins.

classes.title: Bondi, subte, tacho
classes.summary: The bondi, the sacred cola, and a surprisingly old subte

pages.text: The city bus is the **colectivo**, but everyone calls it **bondi**. And porteños invented it.

pages.prompt: How was the colectivo born, in 1928?
options: Taxi drivers began sharing their cars
The city bought old buses from London
A tram company swapped rails for trucks
pages.explain: Taxi drivers short on customers charged each passenger a fixed fare along a route. Soon they stretched the cars to fit more seats.

pages.text: The bondi only stops if you ask. When your line comes, stick your arm out, or it drives right past you.
At the stop, people line up along the wall: **la cola**. It's sacred. Cut it and the whole line will let you know: **“¡Hay cola, eh!”**
Taxis are black and yellow, and porteños call them **tachos**.

pages.prompt: The **subte**, Buenos Aires' metro, opened in 1913. Which of these is younger?
pages.explain: Madrid's opened in 1919. The subte was the first metro in all of Latin America.

pages.text: On the bondi and not sure where to get off? Ask the driver **“¿Me avisás cuando lleguemos a…?”** Most will call out your stop.

classes.title: Obelisco, Colón and a pink house
classes.summary: A monument almost torn down, a pink palace and a café with no rush

pages.text: The **Obelisco** went up in a rush in 1936, and plenty of porteños hated it.

pages.prompt: A few years later, what did the city council vote to do with it?
pages.explain: They voted to demolish it, and the mayor vetoed the decision. Today it's where the whole city goes to celebrate a World Cup, or to protest.

pages.text: It stands on **Avenida 9 de Julio**, which porteños proudly call the widest avenue in the world. Crossing on foot usually takes more than one green light.
The president's office is the **Casa Rosada**. The popular story: President **Sarmiento** had it painted pink to mix the red and white of two rival parties.

pages.prompt: There's a messier theory for the pink. What?
pages.explain: The story goes that the lime paint was mixed with cow's blood, a trick against the damp. Nobody can prove either story, and the red-and-white one is nicer.

pages.text: Singers and conductors rank the **Teatro Colón** among the best opera houses in the world for its sound. The cheapest seats, way up top, are called **el paraíso**: paradise.
At a classic café like the **Tortoni**, order a **cortado** and stay two hours. The waiter won't bring the check until you ask. Bringing it early would feel like kicking you out.

classes.title: Five things you'll notice in your first week
classes.summary: Therapy talk, dog packs, a street that never sleeps, and ¡ojo!

pages.text: A Soda Stereo song calls Buenos Aires **la ciudad de la furia**, the city of fury. Fast, loud, horns honking. Most of that fury is noise, not danger.

pages.prompt: Buenos Aires has more of one profession per person than almost anywhere. Which?
pages.explain: **Hacer terapia** is no secret here. **“Lo hablo con mi psicóloga”** is a normal thing to say at dinner.

pages.text: In Palermo or Recoleta you'll meet a **paseaperros**, a dog walker, dragged along by a whole pack of dogs at once. The pack gets the sidewalk.
Avenida **Corrientes** is the city's Broadway: theaters, bookshops open late, pizza at midnight. People call it **la calle que nunca duerme**, the street that never sleeps.

pages.prompt: **El Ateneo Grand Splendid**, often called one of the world's most beautiful bookshops, used to be something else. What?
pages.explain: An old theater, turned bookshop. The café sits right on the old stage.

pages.text: The thief to know is the **motochorro**, who snatches phones from the back of a motorbike. Porteños aren't paranoid, just alert. Keep your phone off café tables by the street.
The word you'll hear most in your first week: **¡Ojo!**, literally “eye!”. It means watch out. **“¡Ojo con el celu!”** Careful with your phone.

sections.title: Las provincias
sections.summary: Argentina beyond Buenos Aires, from the salt flats to the end of the world

classes.title: Buenos Aires is not Argentina
classes.summary: A huge country, 23 provinces with their own pride, and a map that reaches Antarctica

pages.text: Argentina is huge: roughly five times France. From **La Quiaca** on the Bolivian border down to **Ushuaia**, you get high desert, jungle, vineyards, the flat pampa and glaciers.
There are 23 **provincias**, plus the city of Buenos Aires. Each province has its own governor, constitution, police and flag.

pages.prompt: On the official map every Argentine kid learns at school, which province is the biggest?
pages.explain: School maps include the slice of **Antarctica** that Argentina claims, and it belongs to Tierra del Fuego. Leave the ice out and Buenos Aires wins.

pages.text: Getting around means the **micro**, the long-distance bus. Twenty hours overnight in a **coche cama**, a seat that folds almost flat, is completely normal.

pages.prompt: About how many Argentines live in and around the city of Buenos Aires?
pages.explain: One in three, in one metro area. No wonder the capital sometimes thinks it *is* the country.

pages.text: Nearly every town throws a **Fiesta Nacional** of something it's proud of: the Poncho in Catamarca, the Sun in San Juan, even the **Salame Quintero** in Mercedes.
Provincial pride runs deep. Tell a girl from Salta who moved to Buenos Aires that she's porteña now, and she'll correct you on the spot.
Meet someone from the provinces? Ask **“¿Y qué extrañás de allá?”**, what do you miss from back home. Then settle in for twenty minutes about the food, the family and the landscape.

classes.title: The Noroeste: Andes, coca and Pachamama
classes.summary: Salta, Jujuy and the most Andean corner of the country

pages.text: Fly two hours north of Buenos Aires and you land in the Andes. **Salta** and **Jujuy** feel closer to Bolivia than to Palermo: adobe villages, llamas, ponchos and Quechua words in everyday Spanish.
In the little town of **Purmamarca** stands the **Cerro de los Siete Colores**, a hill striped red, purple, ochre and green. No paint involved: just layers of different minerals.

pages.prompt: On a bus to Humahuaca, the man next to you has a bulging cheek and offers you leaves from a little bag. What's going on?
options: He's sharing coca leaves for the altitude
He's offering you tobacco to chew
He's selling a herbal tea he grows
pages.explain: Up here lots of people **coquean**: they keep a wad of coca leaves in their cheek for hours against altitude, cold and tiredness. Taking a few is fine. So is **no, gracias**.

pages.text: It's no scandal: Argentine law says chewing coca leaves is not drug use. A few leaves in your cheek are a world away from cocaine, which is very much illegal.
Every **1 de agosto** the Andes honor the **Pachamama**, Mother Earth. Families dig a hole and “feed” it with food, coca, corn beer and wine, to thank her and ask for a good year.

pages.prompt: That same morning, all over Argentina, even in Buenos Aires, many people take a shot of something on an empty stomach. What?
options: Caña with rue, against winter's bad luck
Hot mate with salt, against the flu
Red wine with honey, for money
pages.explain: **Caña con ruda**: cane liquor steeped with rue, the herb. One shot on 1 August keeps the bad luck of winter away, or so they say.

pages.text: Jujuy's carnival starts by digging up a cloth devil from a pile of stones: the **desentierro del diablo**. The whole town parties until he's buried again.

classes.title: Cuyo: wine, water and the siesta
classes.summary: Mendoza, Malbec and the highest mountain outside Asia

pages.text: **Cuyo** is Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis: dry land at the foot of the Andes. It barely rains. Yet Mendoza's streets are lined with huge, shady trees.

pages.prompt: How does a desert city keep all those trees alive?
options: Open ditches carry snowmelt to every street
They're desert trees that need no water
pages.explain: Water from the Andes runs through **acequias**, open channels along the curb. The system goes back to the **Huarpe** people, before the Spanish.

pages.text: Walking home at night, mind your step. Falling into an acequia is a rite of passage, and the locals will laugh, kindly.
Mendoza makes most of Argentina's wine. Touring **bodegas** (wineries) by bike is a local classic. At dinner just order **un tinto**, a red: odds are it's Malbec.

pages.prompt: Malbec is Argentina's flagship grape. Where does it originally come from?
pages.explain: From southwest France. It struggled back home and found its real home here, in sun, altitude and dry air.

pages.text: The grape harvest ends with the **Fiesta de la Vendimia**, in early March: parades, a huge show in the hills, and a harvest queen chosen from the queens of the province's 18 departments.
Behind the city stands the **Aconcagua**: almost 7,000 meters, the highest mountain outside Asia. You don't need to climb it. On the road to Chile you can see its snowy face.
In Buenos Aires the **siesta** is a weekend luxury. Here it's the schedule: shops shut after lunch and reopen late in the afternoon, and the summer streets go silent.

classes.title: Córdoba: fernet, cuarteto and the tonada
classes.summary: The province that talks slower, parties harder and jokes about everything

pages.text: You'll hear a cordobés before you see one. The **tonada** stretches the syllable before the stressed one: **“cordoobés”**. Porteños love imitating it. Cordobeses love telling them they do it badly.
Córdoba's nickname is **La Docta**, the learned one. The Jesuits founded the country's oldest university here, and the city is still full of students from all over Argentina.

pages.prompt: In Italy, fernet is a bitter shot after dinner. How does Córdoba drink it?
options: With Coca-Cola, in a tall glass
pages.explain: **Fernet con coca**, lots of ice and a proper foam on top: the drink of every party. Bitter the first time, addictive by the third.

pages.text: Argentina drinks more fernet than any other country, and Córdoba leads the way: the province is said to drink around a third of it. Pace yourself.
Saturday night means a **baile de cuarteto**, Córdoba's own party music. The crowd dances in a giant circle round the floor, and you just follow it.

pages.prompt: Up in Córdoba's hills, **Villa General Belgrano** throws Argentina's big Oktoberfest. Who helped make it a German town?
pages.explain: In 1939 the warship **Graf Spee** was scuttled off Montevideo. Its crew was interned in Argentina, and some sailors settled in these hills for good.

pages.text: Cordobeses are famous for their humor. Their signature word is **culiao**. Vulgar and an insult when angry, between friends it means “dude”. Wait until they call *you* culiao before you try it.

classes.title: The Litoral: rivers, falls and chamamé
classes.summary: Iguazú, Guaraní, Rosario and a very loud yell

pages.text: **Litoral** means coast, but none of it touches the sea. Its coasts are the banks of huge rivers: the **Paraná** and the **Uruguay**.
Up in **Misiones** the soil is bright red and the air is thick and humid. In the jungle stand the stone ruins of **Jesuit missions**, where thousands of Guaraní once lived.

pages.prompt: Iguazú's falls sit on the border with Brazil. What share of them is on the Argentine side?
pages.explain: Roughly 80% of the falls are Argentine. Brazilians will point out that their side has the better panoramic view. Both are right.

pages.text: The star is the **Garganta del Diablo**, a horseshoe of thundering water. The story goes that Eleanor Roosevelt saw Iguazú and sighed: “Poor Niagara!”
The northeast is Guaraní land, and you can hear it. In **Corrientes**, Guaraní is an official language next to Spanish. A kid there is a **gurí**, not a pibe.
The Litoral's music is **chamamé**: accordion, guitar, and couples dancing in a tight embrace. Every January, Corrientes throws a huge national chamamé festival.

pages.prompt: At a chamamé dance, the man next to you throws his head back and lets out a long, piercing scream. What's happening?
options: He's letting out a yell of joy
He's calling his friends over to dance
He's telling the band to play faster
pages.explain: It's a **sapucai**, a Guaraní yell of joy, grief or courage. Nobody expects you to do one. But if you try, go loud.

pages.text: **Rosario**, Argentina's third city, lives by the Paraná. Walk the riverfront and order a **liso**, a draft beer in a straight glass. Rosarinos will remind you that Messi was born here.

pages.prompt: Rosario is hundreds of kilometers from the sea. Where do rosarinos go to the beach on a hot Sunday?
options: A lagoon in the pampa nearby
pages.explain: Little boats cross the river to the islands opposite the city, with sand, trees and a grill. And there are river beaches right in town.

classes.title: Patagonia: ice, wind and Welsh tea
classes.summary: Glaciers, Welsh tea, chocolate and the end of the world

pages.text: **Patagonia** covers more than a quarter of Argentina, yet hardly anyone lives there. Steppe, lakes, mountains and a wind that never stops. The tourists are the ones chasing their hats.
Near **El Calafate**, the **Perito Moreno** glacier ends in a towering wall of ice. For years it kept building an ice bridge across the lake, and each collapse was broadcast live on TV.

pages.prompt: For decades, what made the Perito Moreno famous among glaciers?
options: It wasn't shrinking, unlike most others
It was the fastest-growing in the world
Its ice was bright pink in summer
pages.explain: It stayed stable while others melted. Bad news: since 2019 it has been retreating fast, and scientists doubt it will ever build that ice bridge again.

pages.text: In 1865 a small ship brought a group of **Welsh** settlers to the Chubut valley. Their towns, chapels and tea houses are still there.

pages.prompt: Why did those Welsh families sail all the way to Patagonia?
options: To dig for gold in the rivers
To escape a famine back home
pages.explain: At home, English was pushing Welsh aside. Here they could live, pray and teach in Welsh. Some families still speak it.

pages.text: In towns like **Gaiman**, a **té galés** is a meal, not a snack: pots of tea, scones, jams and **torta negra**, a dense fruit cake made to last the winter. Go hungry.

**Bariloche** looks like the Alps, with chocolate shops on every corner. It's also where teens go on their end-of-school trip, the **viaje de egresados**. Every adult has stories. Few will tell you all of them.
At the very bottom of the map, **Ushuaia** calls itself **el fin del mundo**, the end of the world. From here, ships leave for Antarctica.

pages.prompt: Ushuaia has a little steam train, the **Tren del Fin del Mundo**. What was it first built for?
options: Taking prisoners out to cut wood
Hauling gold down from the mines
pages.explain: Ushuaia began as a prison town. The train carried inmates to the forest to cut timber. Today it carries tourists along the same valley.

sections.title: Íconos e inventos
sections.summary: Mafalda, Borges, the birome and a Pope from Flores

classes.title: Mafalda and her gang
classes.summary: The six-year-old who worried about the whole world

pages.text: **Mafalda** is a little girl with a big bow and bigger questions: world peace, the Beatles, and why grown-ups run things so badly. **Quino** drew her from 1964 to 1973.

pages.prompt: Why does Mafalda's name start with M?
options: She was first drawn for an appliance ad
Quino named her after his mother
It's borrowed from an old tango title
pages.explain: Her name had to echo **Mansfield**, a brand of home appliances. The ad never ran, so she got her own comic strip instead.

pages.text: Her mortal enemy? **La sopa**. Mafalda hates soup almost more than war. Lots of readers saw politics in that bowl: everything you're forced to swallow.
Her gang: **Manolito**, obsessed with money at his dad's shop. **Susanita**, who dreams only of a husband and kids. Dreamy **Felipe**. Tiny, political **Libertad**. Every Argentine knows a Susanita.
She's loved far beyond Argentina. In Italy, the novelist **Umberto Eco** introduced her first book and called her an angry little heroine who rejects the world as it is.

pages.prompt: Mafalda has a statue in Buenos Aires. Where?
options: On a bench, on the corner where Quino lived
Outside the Casa Rosada, on Plaza de Mayo
In the lobby of the Teatro Colón
pages.explain: In **San Telmo**, at Chile and Defensa, right by the building where Quino lived. There's always a line for a photo on the bench next to her.

pages.text: Quino died in 2020, one day after Mafalda's birthday. Fans filled her bench in San Telmo with flowers and notes.

classes.title: Comics, cartoons and snow
classes.summary: The first animated film ever, a bird with no wings, and El Eternauta

pages.text: Argentines call cartoons **dibujitos**. And this country made the world's first animated feature film, **El Apóstol**, in 1917: long before *Snow White*.

pages.prompt: What was El Apóstol about?
options: The president setting fire to Buenos Aires
A gaucho crossing the pampa on foot
A talking condor looking for its family
pages.explain: It mocked President Yrigoyen, who flies up to the gods and burns the city to clean out corruption. Sadly, the only copy burned in a studio fire, so nobody can watch it today.

pages.text: **Clemente** is a striped bird with no wings, drawn by **Caloi**. During the 1978 World Cup, he picked a fight with the country's most famous radio commentator.

pages.prompt: What was the fight about?
options: Whether fans should throw paper in the stadiums
Whether the dictator should hand out the cup
pages.explain: The commentator asked fans not to throw **papelitos**, so the country wouldn't look messy. Clemente said **“¡Tiren papelitos, muchachos!”** The stadiums ended up covered in paper.

pages.text: **El Eternauta** began as a comic in 1957. A deadly snowfall covers Buenos Aires, and anyone it touches dies. In 2025 Netflix made it a hit series with **Ricardo Darín**.
The hero isn't one man, it's the group. Its motto, **nadie se salva solo**, nobody saves themselves alone, is quoted at marches and whenever a neighbor needs a hand.
Its writer, **Héctor Oesterheld**, was kidnapped by the dictatorship and never seen again. So were his four daughters. That's why the Eternauta's silhouette appears at human-rights marches.

classes.title: The writers
classes.summary: Borges, Cortázar, Alfonsina and the songs every kid sings

pages.text: The writer every Argentine name-drops is **Jorge Luis Borges**: short, dizzying stories about labyrinths, mirrors and infinite libraries.

pages.prompt: Borges went almost blind. What job did he get around the same time?
options: Film critic for a big newspaper
Head of a school for painters
pages.explain: He called it an irony: all those books, and no eyes to read them. He kept writing by dictating.

pages.text: Borges was nominated for the Nobel again and again, and never won. He's said to have joked that not giving it to him had become a Scandinavian tradition.
**Julio Cortázar**'s novel **Rayuela**, Hopscotch, can be read straight through, or by jumping between chapters along a map he gives you. It made him an idol for students.
**Alfonsina Storni** was a feminist poet of the 1920s. She died in the sea at Mar del Plata, and the song **“Alfonsina y el mar”** keeps her alive.

pages.prompt: **María Elena Walsh** wrote the songs every Argentine kid sings. Her most famous is about Manuelita. Who's Manuelita?
options: A turtle who travels to Paris
A cow who dreams of tango
A girl who talks to the moon
pages.explain: Parents who sang **“Manuelita vivía en Pehuajó…”** as kids now sing it to theirs, word for word. At a kids' party, the adults sing loudest.

classes.title: Inventions and Nobels
classes.summary: A Hungarian's pen, a murder in Necochea, a Nobel's sauce and a heart surgeon

pages.text: In Argentina a ballpoint pen is a **birome**. **László Bíró**, a Hungarian journalist, patented it here in the 1940s with his partner **Juan Jorge Meyne**. Bi-ró plus Me-yne: birome.

pages.prompt: Who was the birome's first big customer?
options: A chain of Buenos Aires banks
pages.explain: Unlike fountain pens, it didn't leak at high altitude. Argentina is so proud that Bíró's birthday is the **Día del Inventor**.

pages.text: In 1892, in the town of **Necochea**, two children were murdered. Their mother blamed a neighbor.

pages.prompt: How did the police crack the case?
options: A bloody fingerprint on a door
A letter in the mother's handwriting
A neighbor who saw her at the window
pages.explain: Using the new system of **Juan Vucetich**, a Croatian immigrant at the La Plata police, the print matched the mother. The first crime in the world solved with fingerprints.

pages.text: In 1914 a Buenos Aires doctor, **Luis Agote**, did one of the first transfusions with blood kept in a flask, not straight from the donor's arm. A pinch of sodium citrate stopped it from clotting.
Argentina has five Nobel prizes. **Luis Leloir** won chemistry for his work on how the body handles sugars.

pages.prompt: The story goes that young Leloir also invented something now on every Argentine table. What?
options: Salsa golf: mayo mixed with ketchup
Dulce de leche sold in a jar
pages.explain: At a golf club in Mar del Plata, so the legend says. Nobody can prove it, and everyone loves telling it.

pages.text: **René Favaloro** spent years as a country doctor in La Pampa. Then, in Cleveland, he helped pioneer the heart **bypass**, now used worldwide. Back home, he built one of the country's top heart hospitals.

classes.title: Modern icons
classes.summary: A Pope who rode the subte, the Generación Dorada, Vilas and two Oscars

pages.text: **Jorge Bergoglio** grew up in **Flores**, Buenos Aires, and as archbishop rode the subte. In 2013 he became **Pope Francis**, the first Pope from the Americas.

pages.prompt: Pope Francis was a card-carrying member of something very Argentine. What?
pages.explain: A paying **socio** of San Lorenzo, and he kept his membership as Pope.

pages.text: At home he divided people: many adored him, others disliked his politics. And as Pope he never came back to visit. People still argue about why.

**Manu Ginóbili**, from **Bahía Blanca**, won four NBA titles with San Antonio and led the **Generación Dorada** to Olympic gold, beating the USA on the way. In a football country, nobody saw it coming.
In 1977 **Guillermo Vilas** had a magical tennis season and won almost everything. He made tennis popular in Argentina.

pages.prompt: So where did the official ranking put Vilas that year?
pages.explain: The computer kept him behind Jimmy Connors. Plenty of Argentines never accepted it, and a Netflix documentary reopened the fight.

pages.text: Argentina has two Oscars for foreign-language film: **La historia oficial** and **El secreto de sus ojos**. The second stars **Ricardo Darín**, the face of Argentine cinema.
A friend says **“¿Vemos una peli de Darín?”** Say yes. *Nueve reinas*, *Relatos salvajes*, *Argentina, 1985*: you're in safe hands.

sections.title: Historia: el nacimiento de un país
sections.summary: From the first peoples to the granary of the world: how Argentina came to be, up to 1930

classes.title: Before Buenos Aires
classes.summary: The first peoples, a silver dream, and a city founded twice

pages.text: Long before the Spanish, this land was full of peoples: **guaraníes** in the northeast, **diaguitas** in the northwest valleys, **mapuches** by the southern Andes, **querandíes** on the pampa. Argentines call them **pueblos originarios**.
Their descendants are still here. Today **12 de octubre** is no longer the “Día de la Raza” but the Day of Respect for Cultural Diversity.

pages.prompt: Buenos Aires means “good airs”. Where did the name really come from?
options: A Virgin that sailors prayed to
The mild climate the explorers found
A port town in southern Spain
pages.explain: Sailors prayed to **Santa María del Buen Ayre** for good winds. The city kept the “good airs” and dropped the rest.

pages.text: In 1536 **Pedro de Mendoza** founded that first **Buen Ayre** on the Río de la Plata. It went badly: hunger, disease and fights with the querandíes. The survivors gave up and left.

pages.prompt: So where did the Buenos Aires that lasted come from?
options: A new fleet sent from Spain
pages.explain: **Juan de Garay** came down the river from Asunción, in today's Paraguay, and founded the city again, this time for good.

pages.text: Even the country's name is a hope. **Argentina** comes from the Latin for silver: the Spanish dreamed of silver mountains here.
The silver was real, but far away in **Potosí**, in today's Bolivia. For two centuries Buenos Aires stayed a small, muddy port, famous mostly for smuggling.

classes.title: A viceroyalty and two British invasions
classes.summary: How a smuggling port became a capital, and threw out the British twice

pages.text: In 1776 Spain made Buenos Aires the capital of a huge **Virreinato**: today's Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia. Overnight, the smuggling port became the boss.
Power sat in the **Cabildo**, the town council. Its white building with arches still stands on **Plaza de Mayo**. Today it's a museum.

pages.prompt: Look closely at the Cabildo today. What happened to it?
options: It lost arches to make room for avenues
It was moved stone by stone from Córdoba
It was built as a church, then converted
pages.explain: The city chopped it twice for new avenues. It went from eleven arches down to five.

pages.text: In 1806 a British force sailed in and took Buenos Aires. Argentines still call it the **invasiones inglesas**.

pages.prompt: The British march in. What does the Spanish viceroy do?
options: Flees the city with the treasury
Leads the defense street by street
Surrenders and swears loyalty to Britain
pages.explain: Viceroy Sobremonte ran, not his finest hour. The British caught the treasure in Luján anyway, and he ended up in Córdoba. The locals had to fight on their own.

pages.text: Locals organized under **Santiago de Liniers** and threw the British out. A year later the British came back, bigger. Porteños fought street by street, and won again.
The story every kid learns: neighbors poured boiling water and oil from the flat rooftops onto British soldiers. Some of it is polished legend. The street fighting was very real.
Two downtown streets remember it: **Reconquista** and **Defensa**. And porteños learned they could beat an empire without Spain. So why keep obeying a viceroy?

classes.title: May and July: the big dates
classes.summary: The Revolución de Mayo, independence in Tucumán, and the streets named after them

pages.text: In 1808 Napoleon invaded Spain and locked up its king. In Buenos Aires a big question landed: if there's no king, who's in charge here?
On **25 de mayo de 1810**, locals removed the viceroy and formed their own government, the **Primera Junta**. That's the **Revolución de Mayo**, and why the main square is **Plaza de Mayo**.

pages.prompt: Every school drawing of that day shows the crowd outside the Cabildo holding the same thing. What?
pages.explain: A sea of umbrellas, in the rain. Historians have doubts: umbrellas were a pricey import back then, so the picture is probably exaggerated.

pages.text: Not quite independence yet: the Junta still ruled in the Spanish king's name, at least on paper. The real break took six more years of war.

pages.prompt: Where was independence finally declared?
options: In a family house in Tucumán
In the Cabildo of Buenos Aires
pages.explain: Delegates from the provinces met in **San Miguel de Tucumán** and declared independence on **9 de julio de 1816**.

pages.text: That house is now the **Casa Histórica**, a museum and the classic school trip. Almost every Argentine kid has a photo in front of its door.
Both days are **feriados**. People pin a blue-and-white **escarapela** to their chest, and schoolkids act out 1810 in colonial costume, with mustaches drawn on in burnt cork.
The dates are on the map too. **Avenida 9 de Julio** is the huge one with the Obelisco, and almost every town has a street called 25 de Mayo.

classes.title: San Martín, Belgrano and the flag
classes.summary: The man who made the flag and the general who crossed the Andes

pages.text: **Manuel Belgrano** was a lawyer and economist who ended up a general. By the river in **Rosario** he raised a light blue and white flag. Buenos Aires wasn't thrilled: it looked too independent.
Kids learn the **celeste** and white come from the sky and its clouds. Some historians aren't so sure.

pages.prompt: What's the rival theory about the flag's colors?
options: They were the Spanish royal family's colors
They copied a British regiment's uniform
They came from the old Inca empire
pages.explain: Some argue celeste and white were colors of the Borbón royal house. Nobody can prove either story.

pages.text: Belgrano gave nearly everything to the cause and died poor. The day he died, **20 de junio**, is now **Día de la Bandera**, Flag Day.
**José de San Martín** had a bold plan: beat Spain in Peru by going through Chile. From **Mendoza** he led an army over Andes passes more than 4,000 meters high.
With thousands of men, mules and horses, he crossed the **cordillera**, helped free Chile, then Peru. Argentines call him the **Padre de la Patria**.

pages.prompt: San Martín died in France. Where is he today?
pages.explain: His remains came home. His tomb in the **Catedral** on Plaza de Mayo is guarded by **Granaderos** in old blue uniforms, the regiment he founded.

pages.text: Every town has a San Martín street, square or statue, usually on horseback. If you're lost, head for the plaza: he's probably in the middle.

classes.title: Unitarios, federales and gauchos
classes.summary: Decades of civil war, Rosas, and the horsemen of the pampa

pages.text: Independence was the easy part. Then came decades of civil war. **Unitarios** wanted one strong government in Buenos Aires. **Federales** wanted the provinces to rule themselves, each under its own **caudillo**.
Behind it all: who keeps the money from the port? Buenos Aires had a clear answer: Buenos Aires.
**Juan Manuel de Rosas**, a rich landowner and a federal, ran Buenos Aires for about two decades with near-total power.

pages.prompt: Under Rosas, one color was all but required. Which?
pages.explain: Wearing federal red was the safe choice. His enforcers, the **Mazorca**, terrorized anyone who looked like an opponent.

pages.text: Argentines still argue about him. A bloody tyrant, said liberals like **Sarmiento**. A defender of the country against British and French fleets, say others. Don't raise it at an asado unless you have time.
Out on the pampa lived the **gauchos**: expert horsemen who worked cattle, with knife, poncho, mate and guitar. Governments treated them as vagrants and forced many into the army.

pages.prompt: So what turned the gaucho into a national hero?
options: A long poem about one of them
A tango about life on the pampa
pages.explain: **Martín Fierro**, by **José Hernández**, tells of a gaucho dragged to the frontier who ends up an outlaw. Every kid reads it at school.

pages.text: Hernández's birthday, **10 de noviembre**, is the **Día de la Tradición**. Towns like **San Antonio de Areco** fill with horses, ponchos and folk music.
The most quoted lines: **“Los hermanos sean unidos, porque esa es la ley primera.”** Brothers, stick together. Argentines still say it, usually in the middle of a family fight.

classes.title: The Campaña del Desierto
classes.summary: A plan to fill the country, and a war over land still argued about

pages.text: After Rosas fell, a **Constitución** was written in 1853. The new leaders' motto: **gobernar es poblar**, to govern is to populate. Bring immigrants, railways and money.
The plan also meant taking land. In the late 1800s, the army under **Julio Argentino Roca** took the pampa and Patagonia from the **mapuche**, **ranquel**, **tehuelche** and other peoples.

pages.prompt: Official history called it the Campaña del **Desierto**, the desert campaign. Why that name?
options: It painted a lived-in land as empty
The land was mostly sand dunes
pages.explain: Those lands were home to whole peoples. Calling them “desert” made taking them sound like settling nothing.

pages.text: Thousands were killed. Thousands more were taken prisoner, families split up, and many forced to work on farms or as servants. The land went to a few big owners.
For a long time schools taught it as a heroic conquest. Today many historians and indigenous communities call it a **genocidio**. Others reject that word. Many now write the name in quotes.
Roca was on the old 100-peso bill, and his statues stand in many towns. Who belongs on money and pedestals is part of the same argument.

pages.prompt: In a town square you see a statue of Roca. What's likely to have happened to it lately?
options: Splashed with red paint, then cleaned again
Moved indoors to a history museum
Covered in flowers every Día de la Tradición
pages.explain: His statues get painted, cleaned and painted again. Some want them gone, others want them kept. It's the same debate, in the street.

classes.title: The boats: immigrants and conventillos
classes.summary: Millions of Europeans, one room per family, and the mix that made Buenos Aires

pages.text: From the 1870s on, ships brought millions of Europeans, mostly **italianos** and **españoles**. For a while, around half of Buenos Aires was born abroad.
Hence the old joke: Mexicans descend from the Aztecs, Peruvians from the Incas, and Argentines… **from the boats**.

pages.prompt: In Buenos Aires, what do people usually call a man from Madrid?
pages.explain: Galicia sent so many people that **gallego** came to mean any Spaniard. Italians are **tanos**. Both usually affectionate. Usually.

pages.text: New arrivals could sleep free for a few days at the **Hotel de Inmigrantes**, by the port, while they looked for work. Today it's a museum, and people search its records for their great-grandparents.
Many ended up in **conventillos**: old houses split into single rooms, one family per room, one patio and bathroom for dozens. Italians, Spaniards, Jews, Arabs and locals, all together.

pages.prompt: In 1907, tenants all over Buenos Aires went on a rent strike. What did women and kids march with?
pages.explain: Brooms, to “sweep away” the landlords. That patio life, with its fights and its songs, fed the city's slang and its tango.

pages.text: The boats still matter. Lots of Argentines hunt down a great-grandparent's papers to get an Italian or Spanish passport. The lines at the consulates are legendary.

classes.title: The granary of the world
classes.summary: Trains, wheat, the secret vote, rooftop radio, and the coup that ended it all

pages.text: Around 1900 Argentina shipped wheat, corn and beef across the ocean, mostly to Britain. It proudly called itself **el granero del mundo**: the world's granary.
British money built the railways. Look at the map: the lines fan out from Buenos Aires like the ribs of a fan, all carrying grain and cattle to one port.
Around the 1910 centenary, many felt they lived in one of the richest countries on earth. The **Teatro Colón** opened. But the best land sat in a few hands.

pages.prompt: It's 1905 and you walk into a polling station. How do you vote?
options: Out loud, in front of everyone
By raising your hand in a hall
pages.explain: The **voto cantado**, the sung vote: you said your choice aloud, with the local boss listening. Fraud was routine.

pages.text: In 1912 the **Ley Sáenz Peña** made voting secret and compulsory for men. That's why voting is still compulsory in Argentina today. Women had to wait decades more.

pages.prompt: In 1920, four friends climbed onto a theater roof in Buenos Aires. What did they do up there?
pages.explain: They broadcast Wagner's *Parsifal* to a few dozen homemade radio sets: one of the world's first public broadcasts.

pages.text: They're remembered as **los locos de la azotea**, the rooftop madmen. Argentina still celebrates that day as Broadcasting Day.
Then came the 1929 crash, and grain and beef prices sank. Soon the army overthrew President **Yrigoyen**: the first of many coups, and the end of the granary years.

sections.title: Historia: el siglo XX y hoy
sections.summary: Perón, the dictatorship, Malvinas, 2001 and why everyone thinks in dollars

classes.title: Coups, Perón and Evita
classes.summary: The man who still splits family asados, and the woman millions mourned

pages.text: For half a century, the army overthrew governments again and again. The good news: since 1983 Argentina has had its longest run of democracy ever, and most Argentines guard it fiercely.

**Juan Domingo Perón** was a colonel in the government of the 1943 coup. As labor secretary he backed the unions: pensions, paid holidays, labor courts. Many workers felt they finally had a friend up high.

pages.prompt: In 1945 Perón's rivals forced him out and locked him up on an island. What got him out?
options: A secret deal with the navy
A ruling from the Supreme Court
pages.explain: On **17 de octubre**, workers marched into the square and demanded him back. Some cooled their tired feet in the fountains, an image that became legend.

pages.text: That night Perón spoke from the balcony of the Casa Rosada. Peronists still celebrate 17 October as the **Día de la Lealtad**, Loyalty Day.

**Evita**, a young actress from a small town, married Perón. Her foundation built hospitals and schools, and she pushed the law that gave women the vote. She died at 33. Millions queued for days to say goodbye.
Opponents sneered at Perón's supporters as **descamisados**, the shirtless ones. Perón and Evita turned the insult into a badge of pride.

pages.prompt: Peronists have an animal nickname for anti-Peronists. Which animal?
pages.explain: **Gorila**. It's a jab, so keep it for when you know the room. Anti-Peronists have their own names for Peronists, too.

pages.text: A 1955 coup threw Perón out and banned Peronism for almost two decades. He came back, won again and died in office. For fans, social justice. For critics, censorship and a personality cult.
The divide is **la grieta**, the crack, and it runs right through the family asado. Plenty of families have a no-politics rule at Sunday lunch. Respect it.

classes.title: The last dictatorship
classes.summary: 1976–1983: the disappeared, the Madres and Abuelas, and “Nunca más”

pages.text: After Perón died came chaos: guerrilla attacks, far-right death squads, a failing economy. On **24 de marzo de 1976** a military junta led by **Jorge Rafael Videla** seized power.

The regime hunted anyone it called “subversive”: guerrillas, but also union delegates, students, lawyers, teenagers. People were kidnapped, taken to secret centers like the **ESMA**, tortured, and most were murdered.
Families got no body and no answer. The victims became **los desaparecidos**, the disappeared. Human rights groups speak of 30,000. The regime destroyed its records, so a full count may never exist.

pages.prompt: In 1977, mothers of the disappeared met in Plaza de Mayo. Gatherings were banned, and police told them to move along. What did they do?
options: Kept walking in pairs around the monument
Moved their meetings into a church nearby
Went home and wrote letters abroad
pages.explain: Standing still was a gathering. Walking wasn't. So they walked, with white headscarves on their heads.

pages.text: They're the **Madres de Plaza de Mayo**, and they still walk there on Thursday afternoons. Their white **pañuelo** is painted on the ground around the square's monument.
Babies born to prisoners were handed to other families under false names. The **Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo**, the grandmothers, have searched for them ever since.

pages.prompt: With the parents gone, how could the Abuelas prove a young person was their grandchild?
options: A DNA test using the grandparents' blood
Birth records kept secretly by nurses
pages.explain: They helped push scientists to create a “grandparent” DNA test. Each **nieto restituido**, a grandchild who gets their identity back, makes national news.

pages.text: In 1985 civilian judges put the junta leaders on trial. The prosecutor closed with **“Señores jueces: nunca más.”** Videla got life. The film *Argentina, 1985* tells that story.
Every 24 March, the **Día de la Memoria**, hundreds of thousands march to Plaza de Mayo with photos of the disappeared: **Memoria, Verdad y Justicia**.

classes.title: Malvinas
classes.summary: The 1982 war, the young soldiers, and a claim nearly every Argentine shares

pages.text: The **Islas Malvinas** sit in the South Atlantic, off Patagonia. Britain has held them since 1833 and Argentina has claimed them ever since. Here, always say **Malvinas**, never Falklands.
In 1982 the dictatorship faced a collapsing economy and growing protests. On **2 de abril** its troops landed on the islands, and crowds cheered in Plaza de Mayo. Britain sent a fleet.

pages.prompt: Who made up most of Argentina's troops on the islands?
options: Career soldiers with years of training
Volunteers who signed up after the landing
pages.explain: Most were **conscriptos** of 18 or 19, barely out of school, sent to freezing trenches, often underfed and badly equipped.

pages.text: 649 Argentines died. Almost half of them went down with one ship, the cruiser **General Belgrano**.

pages.prompt: During the war, what did most people at home hear from the news?
pages.explain: Censored news and magazines kept saying **“estamos ganando”**, we're winning, almost until the surrender in June. The shock turned into fury, and the junta fell. Democracy came back in 1983.

pages.text: Today 2 April is a national holiday for the **ex combatientes** and **los caídos**, the veterans and the fallen. For years many veterans felt forgotten, and the wounds are still an open subject.

You'll see **“Las Malvinas son argentinas”** on road signs, murals and buses. The claim is one of the few things almost everyone agrees on. The war is different: most see it as the dictatorship's doomed gamble.
If it comes up, listen more than you argue. Plenty of Argentines have a relative or neighbor who fought there.

classes.title: Democracy, hyperinflation and 2001
classes.summary: From Alfonsín to “que se vayan todos”

pages.text: In 1983 democracy returned with **Raúl Alfonsín**. His promise is still quoted: **“con la democracia se come, se cura y se educa”**. With democracy, people eat, heal and learn.
The economy didn't cooperate. By the end of the decade prices went wild: yearly inflation passed 3,000%. Supermarkets relabeled prices several times a day.

pages.prompt: It's 1989 and you just got paid. What's the smart move?
options: Spend it all that same day
Put it in a savings account
Keep it at home for next month
pages.explain: Money lost value in your pocket by the hour. People ran to the supermarket on payday, a reflex some Argentines still have.

pages.text: In 1991 a law fixed it: **one peso = one dollar**, the **convertibilidad**. Inflation fell to almost zero. The decade brought cheap imports and cheap trips abroad.
The hangover came later: factories closed, unemployment passed 18%, debt piled up to keep the peg alive. That decade still splits dinner tables.
December 2001: people rushed to pull out their savings, so the government capped withdrawals. That's the **corralito**. The middle class hit the streets banging pots: the **cacerolazo**.

pages.prompt: The protests brought down President De la Rúa, who fled the Casa Rosada by helicopter. How many presidents did Argentina have in about twelve days?
pages.explain: Five presidents came and went. The chant on every street was **“¡Que se vayan todos!”**: out with all of them.

pages.text: Then the one-to-one peso ended, and the devaluation wiped out much of people's savings. A whole generation learned never to fully trust a bank again.

classes.title: Money today: thinking in dollars
classes.summary: Inflation, the dólar blue, arbolitos and cash under the mattress

pages.text: After all that, Argentines live by one rule: pesos to spend, dollars to save. Plenty of savings sit at home in cash, **bajo el colchón**, under the mattress.

pages.prompt: You're buying a flat in Palermo. How is it usually paid for?
options: In US dollars, often counted in cash
pages.explain: Flats and cars are priced in dollars (**U$S**), and it's common for the notes to be counted on the spot at signing.

pages.text: Inflation even ate the money itself. Your Argentine grandparents may have used five different currencies, each one born by chopping zeros off the last.
For years buying dollars was capped, so a parallel market boomed: the **dólar blue**. At one point there were over a dozen dollar rates, even a **dólar Coldplay** for concert tickets.

pages.prompt: On calle Florida, a man keeps muttering “Cambio, cambio.” Locals call him an **arbolito**, a little tree. Why, the story goes?
options: He stands in the same spot all day, like a tree
He hides behind street trees from the police
The first ones worked out of a city park
pages.explain: He's a street money changer. He'll walk you to a **cueva**, a “cave”: the back office where the swap happens.

pages.text: Since 2025 anyone can buy dollars freely again. The habit stays: **¿A cuánto está el dólar?** is small talk, like the weather.
Before you pay, ask. Many shops give a discount for **efectivo** (cash) or transfer. When they ask **“¿Efectivo o tarjeta?”**, the answer can change the price.
